content:
The table in question is essentially the “Contents” or index for Amendment A2:2014 to EN 1995-1-1:2004 (Eurocode 5 “Design of timber structures – Part 1-1: General – Common rules and rules for buildings”), as adopted and published by Standard Norge in February 2024. It lists twenty discrete modifications to the base Eurocode text, plus the foreword. Each entry identifies:

 •  A sequential item number (1 to 20)  
 •  The clause or sub-clause of EN 1995-1-1 subject to amendment (for example “1.2”, “6.1.5”, “8.7.1” or “B.4”)  
 •  A brief description of the topic or title of that clause (e.g. “Normative references”, “Torsion”, “Plate anchorage capacity”)  
 •  The page in the amendment document where the modification appears  

More specifically:

1.  Foreword – introductory material and status information (page 3).  
2.  Item 1: Modifications to clause 1.2 “Normative references” (page 4).  
3.  Item 2: Modification to clause 1.6 “Symbols used in EN 1995-1-1” (page 4).  
4.  Item 3: Modifications to clause 2.2.3 “Serviceability limit states” (page 4).  
5.  Item 4: Modification to clause 2.3.2.2 “Load-duration and moisture influences on deformations” (page 4).  
6.  Item 5: Modification to clause 4.2 “Resistance to corrosion” (page 5).  
7.  Item 6: Modification to clause 6.1.5 “Compression perpendicular to the grain” (page 5).  
8.  Item 7: Modification to clause 6.1.8 “Torsion” (page 5).  
9.  Item 8: Modification to clause 6.2.3 “Combined bending and axial tension” (page 5).  
10. Item 9: Modification to clause 6.5.2 “Beams with a notch at the support” (page 6).  
11. Item 10: Modification to clause 8.3.2 “Axially loaded nails” (page 6).  
12. Item 11: Modifications to clause 8.4 “Stapled connections” (page 6).  
13. Item 12: Modification to clause 8.6 “Dowelled connections” (page 6).  
14. Item 13: Modifications to clause 8.7.1 “Laterally loaded screws” (page 7).  
15. Item 14: Modification to clause 8.7.2 “Axially loaded screws” (page 7).  
16. Item 15: Modifications to clause 8.8.5.1 “Plate anchorage capacity” (page 8).  
17. Item 16: Modification to clause 8.8.5.2 “Plate capacity” (page 8).  
18. Item 17: Modification to clause 8.9 “Split ring and shear plate connectors” (page 9).  
19. Item 18: Modification to clause 8.10 “Toothed-plate connectors” (page 9).  
20. Item 19: Modifications to Annex A (page 10).  
21. Item 20: Modification to clause B.4 “Maximum shear stress” (page 10).  

This index allows a user—or an automated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline—to quickly locate which parts of the original Eurocode text have been altered: from global references and symbol definitions, through serviceability and durability provisions, to very specific structural connection and component rules (nails, screws, dowels, plates, etc.), and finally to corrections in the normative annexes. Each row ties a discrete technical topic back to its exact location in the amendment, providing a high-granularity roadmap for ingesting or retrieving the revised passages.

 The standard assumes the use of a number of parameters to be determined nationally, denoted Nationally Determined Parameters or NDP, given in a National Annex to the standard, NA. The standard can only be used for the design of load-bearing structures together with the nationally determined parameters applicable in the country where a structure or a product is to be used. The standard, therefore, can only be used as a basis for design of structures or products to be used in Norway together with the requirements given in the Norwegian national annex to the standard. The standard specifies recommended values for the nationally determined parameters, these can not be used as replacement for the nationally determined parameters.
 National Annexes are in principle informative. According to §10-2 in the Technical Regulations to the Planning and Building Act (pbl) the essential requirements to mechanical resistance and stability, including geotechnichs, may be met by design of structures in accordance with Norwegian Standard NS- EN 1990 Eurocode: Basis of structural design and underlying standards in the series NS-EN 1991 to NS- EN 1999, with their National Annexes. metadata.sections: 6  Modification to 6.1.5, Compression perpendicular to the grain

content:
The supplied Table 8.5 defines the minimum axial spacings and edge- or end-distances that must be maintained when placing dowels into a solid wood member.  It is organized into three columns:

 1. “Spacing and edge/end distances (see Figure 8.7)”  
    – Identifies six distance parameters, labeled a₁ through a₄ with subscript “t” (loaded) or “c” (unloaded), and describes their geometric meaning:  
      • a₁ – spacing parallel to the grain  
      • a₂ – spacing perpendicular to the grain  
      • a₃,t – end distance on the loaded side of the dowel  
      • a₃,c – end distance on the unloaded side of the dowel  
      • a₄,t – edge distance on the loaded side of the dowel  
      • a₄,c – edge distance on the unloaded side of the dowel  

 2. “Angle to grain (α)”  
    – Specifies, for each distance measure, the range of the dowel’s axis orientation α relative to the wood grain direction.  Angles are measured in degrees, from 0° through 360°, with positive rotations defined consistently (see Figure 8.7).  

 3. “Minimum spacings and edge/end distances”  
    – Gives the required minimum distance as a function of the dowel diameter d and the angle α.  Where two expressions are compared, the larger value governs.

Detailed breakdown of each row:

• a₁ (parallel to grain)  
  – Applies for all α from 0° to 360°.  
  – Minimum spacing = (3 + 2·|cos α|) · d  
    • When the dowel axis aligns exactly with the grain (α = 0° or 180°), |cos α| = 1 ⇒ spacing = 5 d  
    • When perpendicular (α = 90°, 270°), |cos α| = 0 ⇒ spacing = 3 d  
    • Interpolates continuously between these extremes.

• a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
  – Applies for all α from 0° to 360°.  
  – Minimum spacing = 3 · d  
    • Independent of α.

• a₃,t (loaded end)  
  – Applicable when the dowel’s axis is tilted against the loaded end: –90° ≤ α ≤ +90°.  
  – Minimum end distance = max(7 · d; 80 mm)  
    • Ensures a generous bearing length under end loading.

• a₃,c (unloaded end)  
  – Broken into three α-ranges:  
    1. 90° ≤ α ≤ 150°: end distance = a₃,t · |sin α|  
    2. 150° ≤ α ≤ 210°: end distance = max(3.5 · d; 40 mm)  
    3. 210° ≤ α ≤ 270°: end distance = a₃,t · |sin α|  
  – For angles near transverse to the grain, the |sin α| factor reduces required distance; for near-axial (around 180°) orientation, a fixed minimum governs.

• a₄,t (loaded edge)  
  – Applies for 0° ≤ α ≤ 180°.  
  – Minimum edge distance = max((2 + 2·sin α) · d; 3 · d)  
    • When the dowel is perpendicular to the edge (α = 90°), sin α = 1 ⇒ expression = 4 d (which exceeds 3 d).  
    • When parallel (α = 0° or 180°), sin α = 0 ⇒ expression = 2 d, but the 3 d floor applies.

• a₄,c (unloaded edge)  
  – Applies for 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°.  
  – Minimum edge distance = 3 · d  

Notes on variables:  
– d is the nominal dowel diameter.  
– α is measured between the dowel axis and the grain direction in the plane of the wood, following the convention in Figure 8.7.  

Contextual linkage:  
In structural fastener design (see modifications to Section 8.7.1 on laterally loaded screws), an analogous approach is used to determine minimum spacings and edge distances: the “effective diameter” dₑₓ𝘵 (reflecting the loaded thread core) replaces d when calculating capacities, but the outer diameter still governs spacing and edge-distance requirements.  Rows a₁ through a₄ in Table 8.5 thus serve as a model for similar provisions in screw design.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the replacement Table 8.7 (“Minimum spacings and edge and end distances for ring and shear connectors”), suitable for capturing in a RAG-style vector store. Wherever possible, we spell out notation, define variables, and call out piecewise intervals in plain text.

1. Table Purpose and Context  
   • Specifies the minimum center-to-center spacings (and distances to free edges or ends) required for dowels, ring connectors and shear dowels in timber elements.  
   • All distances are expressed as multiples of the connector’s characteristic diameter, dₙ (denoted d_c in the table).  
   • The angle α is the orientation of the connector’s axis relative to the grain direction (0° means perfectly parallel to grain; 90° is perpendicular).  
   • A reference “Figure 8.7” defines the geometric setup and shows how each clearance dimension a_i is measured.

2. Notation Key  
   • a₁, a₂, a₃,ₜ, a₃,꜀, a₄,ₜ, a₄,꜀: distinct spacing or edge/end-distance parameters.  
   • α: angle between connector axis and grain direction, in degrees.  
   • d_c: characteristic connector diameter (e.g. shank or hole diameter).  
   • |cos α|, |sin α|: absolute values of the trigonometric functions, ensuring symmetry for positive/negative angles.  
   • Decimal comma notation (e.g. “1,2 d_c”) matches the source’s style.

3. Row-by-Row Summary   

   a) a₁ (parallel to grain)  
     – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360° (applies for any orientation around the grain).  
     – Formula:  
         a₁ = (1,2 + 0,8 · |cos α|) · d_c  
       • When α = 0° or 180° (fully parallel), |cos α| = 1 → a₁ = (1,2 + 0,8)·d_c = 2,0·d_c.  
       • When α = 90° or 270° (perpendicular), |cos α| = 0 → a₁ = 1,2·d_c.

   b) a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
     – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360° (no angular dependency).  
     – Constant:  
         a₂ = 1,2 · d_c  

   c) a₃,ₜ (loaded end distance)  
     – Angle range: –90° ≤ α ≤ 90° (end facing the load).  
     – Constant:  
         a₃,ₜ = 2,0 · d_c  

   d) a₃,꜀ (unloaded end distance)  
     – Piecewise definition over α from 90° to 270°:  
       • For 90° ≤ α ≤ 150° and for 210° ≤ α ≤ 270°:  
            a₃,꜀ = (0,4 + 1,6 · |sin α|) · d_c  
         – Here, the |sin α| term raises the clearance when the end is more perpendicular.  
       • For 150° ≤ α ≤ 210° (mid-span around directly opposite the loaded end):  
            a₃,꜀ = 1,2 · d_c  

   e) a₄,ₜ (loaded edge distance)  
     – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 180° (edge under positive-moment side).  
     – Formula:  
         a₄,ₜ = (0,6 + 0,2 · |sin α|) · d_c  

   f) a₄,꜀ (unloaded edge distance)  
     – Angle range: 180° ≤ α ≤ 360° (edge on the opposite, tension-free side).  
     – Constant:  
         a₄,꜀ = 0,6 · d_c  

4. Design Rationale (brief)  
   • End distances (a₃,ₜ vs. a₃,꜀) are larger on the loaded side to prevent splitting under concentrated forces.  
   • Edge distances (a₄,ₜ) incorporate a small sinusoidal variation to reflect slightly higher risk when the load is perpendicular.  
   • Parallel spacing a₁ also varies with |cos α| because splitting risk grows as the connector axis aligns with the grain.  
   • Unloaded-side distances (a₃,꜀ in certain sectors, a₄,꜀) are smaller, reflecting reduced stress concentration.

5. How to Store in a Vector-Ready Schema  
   • Store each a_i as an object with fields:  
     – “name”: e.g. “a3c”  
     – “description”: e.g. “Unloaded end distance”  
     – “angle_ranges”: list of {min_alpha, max_alpha, formula}  
     – “formula”: plain-text expression, optionally parsed into coefficients and trig terms  
     – “multiplier”: always “d_c”  
   • Index key terms: “spacing,” “edge distance,” “end distance,” “ring connector,” “shear dowel,” and the trig-dependent patterns (“|cos α|,” “|sin α|”).

This detailed breakdown ensures each clearance rule is fully captured—as numeric constants, angle intervals, and functional dependencies—ready for embedding in a RAG vector database and for retrieval in design-code queries.

content:
The table below—Table 8.8—summarizes all of the minimum spacing and edge‐ or end‐distance requirements for toothed‐plate connections (connection types C1 through C9) in timber when using circular plug‐type teeth of diameter d_c.  It is indexed by the specific spacing or edge/end distance (a₁, a₂, a₃,t, a₃,c, a₄,t, a₄,c), the orientation of the load relative to the grain (angle α), and the formula or constant multiple of d_c that yields the required minimum distance.  Designers refer to Figure 8.7 for definitions of these distances on the detail drawing of a plated connection.

1. a₁ (spacing parallel to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360° (i.e. any orientation)  
   – Minimum spacing: (1.2 + 0.3 · |cos α|) · d_c  
   • This formula increases spacing slightly when the load is aligned with the grain (α = 0° or 180°), since |cos α| = 1 gives 1.5 d_c, but reduces it toward 1.2 d_c as the load rotates toward 90° or 270°.

2. a₂ (spacing perpendicular to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum spacing: 1.2 · d_c  
   • Independent of orientation; always 1.2 times the tooth diameter.

3. a₃,t (end‐distance at the loaded end of the plate)  
   – Angle range: –90° ≤ α ≤ 90° (i.e. load directed toward that end)  
   – Minimum distance: 1.5 · d_c  
   • Ensures sufficient timber bearing length in the direction of applied load.

4. a₃,c (end‐distance at the unloaded (compression) end of the plate)  
   – Broken into three α bands:  
     • 90° ≤ α ≤ 150° and 210° ≤ α ≤ 270°:  
       Minimum = (0.9 + 0.6 · |sin α|) · d_c  
       – Peaks at α = 120° or 240° (|sin α| = 0.866), giving ≈1.42 d_c; drops to 0.9 d_c at α = 90° or 270°.  
     • 150° ≤ α ≤ 210°:  
       Minimum = 1.2 · d_c  
       – A constant value for nearly perpendicular reverse loads.

5. a₄,t (edge‐distance at the loaded edge)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 180° (load directed toward that edge)  
   – Minimum distance: (0.6 + 0.2 · |sin α|) · d_c  
   • Ranges from 0.6 d_c (α = 0° or 180°) up to 0.8 d_c at α = 90°.

6. a₄,c (edge‐distance at the unloaded edge)  
   – Angle range: 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum distance: 0.6 · d_c  
   • A constant one‐sized clearance behind the loaded edge, regardless of angle within this half‐circle.

Key points for RAG/vector‐store indexing or metadata:  
- All distances are proportional to the connector’s tooth (plug) diameter d_c.  
- α is measured between the load direction and the grain direction in the timber.  
- Formulas use absolute values of cos α or sin α to capture symmetry in load reversal.  
- Distinctions are made between loaded vs. unloaded ends/edges (a₃,t vs. a₃,c; a₄,t vs. a₄,c) and between parallel vs. perpendicular spacings (a₁ vs. a₂).  
- This table replaces any previous “Table 8.8” in the standard and should be used for all toothed-plate connection checks (C1–C9).

Below is a structured, detailed description of “Table 3.1 – Values of k_mod,” intended to capture its full scope for ingestion into a RAG vector store. The table tabulates the modification factors (k_mod) used to adjust timber-based material design values for different load-duration classes and service classes.  

1. Table Purpose  
• Defines k_mod factors for various timber and wood-based products.  
• Covers five load-duration categories: Permanent action, Long-term, Medium-term, Short-term, and Instantaneous action.  
• Differentiates among three service classes (1, 2, 3) reflecting environmental conditions (temperature, humidity).

2. Materials and Standards  
Each material group is defined by relevant European standards:  
• Solid timber (EN 14081-1)  
• Glued laminated timber (EN 14080)  
• Laminated veneer lumber (LVL; EN 14374, EN 14279)  
• Plywood (EN 636, with Types 1, 2 and 3 per EN 636-1, ‑2, ‑3)  
• Oriented strand board (OSB; EN 300)  
   – OSB/2, OSB/3, OSB/4 variants  
• Particleboard (EN 312)  
   – Types P4, P5, P6, P7  
• Hard fibreboard (EN 622-2)  
   – HB.LA, HB.HLA1/2  
• Medium-density fibreboard (EN 622-3)  
   – MBH.LA1/2, MBH.HLS1/2  
• MDF (EN 622-5)  
   – MDF.LA, MDF.HLS  

3. Service Classes and k_mod Values  
For each material and service class (1, 2, 3), five k_mod values are listed:

Load-duration class  
— Permanent action  
— Long-term action  
— Medium-term action  
— Short-term action  
— Instantaneous action  

General trends:  
• Service class 1 and 2 often share identical k_mod values for a given material.  
• Service class 3 values are generally reduced, especially under permanent and long-term loads.  
• Instantaneous k_mod typically ≥ 1.00 for all material types, reflecting the brief duration’s minimal degradation.  

4. Representative Data Blocks  
Solid Timber (EN 14081-1)  
– Class 1 & 2: [0.60; 0.70; 0.80; 0.90; 1.10]  
– Class 3: [0.50; 0.55; 0.65; 0.70; 0.90]  

Glued Laminated Timber (EN 14080) & LVL (EN 14374/14279)  
– Identical k_mod sets to Solid Timber across service classes.  

Plywood (EN 636)  
– Type 1 & 2 mirror solid timber values.  
– Type 3 (Class 3 only): [0.50; 0.55; 0.65; 0.70; 0.90].  

OSB (EN 300)  
– OSB/2 (class 1): [0.30; 0.45; 0.65; 0.85; 1.10]  
– OSB/3, OSB/4 (class 1): [0.40; 0.50; 0.70; 0.90; 1.10]  
– OSB/3, OSB/4 (class 2): [0.30; 0.40; 0.55; 0.70; 0.90]  

Particleboard (EN 312)  
– P4, P5 (class 1): [0.30; 0.45; 0.65; 0.85; 1.10]  
– P5 (class 2): [0.20; 0.30; 0.45; 0.60; 0.80]  
– P6, P7 (class 1): [0.40; 0.50; 0.70; 0.90; 1.10]  
– P7 (class 2): [0.30; 0.40; 0.55; 0.70; 0.90]  

Fibreboard, Hard (EN 622-2)  
– HB.LA/HB.HLA1-2 (class 1): [0.30; 0.45; 0.65; 0.85; 1.10]  
– HB.HLA1-2 (class 2): [0.20; 0.30; 0.45; 0.60; 0.80]  

Fibreboard, Medium (EN 622-3)  
– MBH.LA1-2 & MBH.HLS1 (class 1): [0.20; 0.40; 0.60; 0.80; 1.10]  
– MBH.HLS1/2 (class 2): [–; –; –; 0.45; 0.80] (dashes indicate not applicable/no data for longer durations)  

Fibreboard, MDF (EN 622-5)  
– MDF.LA, MDF.HLS (class 1): [0.20; 0.40; 0.60; 0.80; 1.10]  
– MDF.HLS (class 2): [–; –; –; 0.45; 0.80]  

5. Usage Notes  
• In structural calculations, multiply characteristic strengths by k_mod to account for load duration and service conditions.  
• Short- and instantaneous actions yield the highest k_mod (close to or above unity). Permanent loads have the lowest factors.  
• Service class 3 (outdoor or high-moisture) consistently shows the greatest reduction in k_mod.  

This exhaustive breakdown preserves the relationships among material type, standard, service class, and load-duration factor, enabling precise lookup and automated indexing in a RAG-enabled system.

Below is a structured, paragraph‐style description of the table you provided (Table 3.2 – Values of k_def for timber and wood‐based materials). You can index this text into a RAG system to allow semantic lookup of any material, standard reference or service‐class value.

Description:

The table presents characteristic modification factors (k_def) for a range of solid timber and engineered wood products, organized by product category, applicable European standard(s), and three service classes. It is titled “Table 3.2 – Values of k_def for timber and wood‐based materials.” The three service classes correspond to increasing levels of humidity and exposure (1 = dry interior, 2 = moderate humidity, 3 = high humidity or exterior).

Columns:
• Material: lists the main product types, including sub-types where relevant  
• Standard: cites the relevant EN (European Norm) number(s) governing specification and testing  
• Service class 1, 2, 3: numerical k_def values for each exposure class; a dash (“–”) indicates the factor is not defined or not applicable for that class

Rows and key entries:

1. Solid timber  
   – Standard: EN 14081-1  
   – k_def: 0.60 in service class 1; 0.80 in class 2; 2.00 in class 3  

2. Glued laminated timber  
   – Standard: EN 14080  
   – k_def: same breakdown as solid timber (0.60 / 0.80 / 2.00)  

3. Laminated veneer lumber (LVL)  
   – Standards: EN 14374 and EN 14279  
   – k_def: 0.60 / 0.80 / 2.00  

4. Plywood (EN 636)  
   – Type EN 636-1: k_def = 0.80 (class 1), not defined for classes 2 and 3  
   – Type EN 636-2: k_def = 0.80 / 1.00 (for classes 1 and 2), not defined for class 3  
   – Type EN 636-3: k_def = 0.80 / 1.00 / 2.50  

5. Oriented strand board (OSB, EN 300)  
   – OSB/2: 2.25 in service class 1; not defined in classes 2 or 3  
   – OSB/3 and OSB/4: 1.50 / 2.25 in classes 1 and 2 respectively; not defined in class 3  

6. Particleboard (EN 312)  
   – Type P4: k_def = 2.25 in class 1; not defined for classes 2 or 3  
   – Type P5: 2.25 in class 1; 3.00 in class 2; – in class 3  
   – Type P6: 1.50 in class 1; – in classes 2 and 3  
   – Type P7: 1.50 in class 1; 2.25 in class 2; – in class 3  

7. Fibreboard, hard (EN 622-2)  
   – HB.LA: 2.25 in class 1; – in classes 2 and 3  
   – HB.HLA1 and HB.HLA2: 2.25 in class 1; 3.00 in class 2; – in class 3  

8. Fibreboard, medium density (EN 622-3)  
   – MBH.LA1 and MBH.LA2: 3.00 in class 1; – in classes 2 and 3  
   – MBH.HLS1 and MBH.HLS2: 3.00 in class 1; 4.00 in class 2; – in class 3  

9. Fibreboard, MDF (EN 622-5)  
   – MDF.LA: 2.25 in class 1; – in classes 2 and 3  
   – MDF.HLS: 2.25 in class 1; 3.00 in class 2; – in class 3  

Summary of key patterns:  
– Solid and glued‐laminated timbers, plus LVL, share the same k_def values across service classes (0.60 / 0.80 / 2.00).  
– Plywood shows incremental increases in higher types and service classes, culminating at 2.50 in class 3 for Type EN 636-3.  
– Panel products (OSB, particleboard, fibreboard) generally have higher k_def in class 1 (≥ 1.50) reflecting reduced structural safety under humid conditions and often drop out (undefined “–”) in class 3.  
– MDF.HLS is notable for having a defined class 2 factor (3.00), whereas the MDF.LA variant does not.

This description encapsulates the table’s structure, materials, standards and k_def values by service class for easy retrieval in a RAG environment.

The layout consists of two main blocks: text and equations at the top, and a two‐part line drawing (“Figure 6.2”) at the bottom.

1. Heading and Context  
• The top of the page continues under the heading “σ_c,90,d = F_c,90,d / A_ef” with equation label (6.3).  
• Immediately below is a “where:” list defining each symbol in (6.3):  
  – σ_c,90,d: design compressive stress in the effective contact area perpendicular to grain  
  – F_c,90,d: design compressive load perpendicular to the grain  
  – A_ef: effective contact area in compression perpendicular to the grain  
  – f_c,90,d: design compressive strength perpendicular to the grain  
  – k_c,90: factor accounting for load configuration, splitting risk, and compressive deformation  

2. Notes on Effective Contact Area  
• A paragraph explains that A_ef should be determined using the effective contact length parallel to the grain. The actual contact length, ℓ, at each end may be increased by 30 mm but not more than a, ℓ, or ℓ/2, with a reference to Figure 6.2.

3. National Choice for k_c,90  
• It states that k_c,90 is normally 1.0 unless national‐annex conditions allow a higher value (up to a specified limit).  
• For continuous supports (ℓ₁ ≥ 2 h), clause (3) prescribes k_c,90 = 1.25 for solid softwood and 1.5 for glued laminated softwood.  
• For discrete supports (ℓ₁ ≥ 2 h), clause (4) prescribes k_c,90 = 1.5 for solid softwood and 1.75 for glued laminated softwood (provided ℓ ≤ 400 mm).  
• It clarifies that h is the member’s depth and ℓ the contact length.

4. Figure 6.2 – Member on (a) Continuous and (b) Discrete Supports  
• Two side–elevation sketches labelled (a) and (b) illustrate a beam under compressive load at supports.  
• In (a) “continuous support”:  
  – The beam rests along its entire bottom face on a support surface.  
  – Downward arrows indicate a uniform strip load over length ℓ adjacent to each end, separated from the support edge by distance a.  
  – Upward reaction arrows are shown along the entire contact region.  
  – A cross-section at midspan shows beam height h and width b.  
  – Dimensions “a,” “ℓ,” and “ℓ₁” are annotated along the beam top.  
• In (b) “discrete support”:

5. Void Paragraphs Note  
At the very top a drafting note states: “Paragraphs (5) to (7), figures 6.3 and 6.4 and expressions (6.5) to (6.10) are void,” indicating that only the shown clauses and figures are currently in force.

Both views are rendered in simple axonometric perspective, with dashed lines indicating hidden back edges and the letter “Z” on the side face marking the shear plane of interest.

1. General layout  
   – Each subfigure shows a rectangular timber block in three-quarter view, with its long axis running into/out of the page.

2. Figure 6.5(a): shear component parallel to the grain  
   – This subfigure corresponds to a shear stress component acting parallel to the grain.

This table (Table 8.6) defines the minimum geometric layout required when designing connections that use axially loaded screws in timber (with or without steel plates). All dimensions are expressed in multiples of the screw’s nominal outer thread diameter, d, and apply provided the timber member thickness t ≥ 12 d. The values refer to spacings between screw centres (a₁ and a₂) and to end- or edge-distances measured to the centre of gravity of the threaded part of each screw (a₁,CG, a₂,CG and a₃,CG). Figure 8.11a illustrates how these are measured in both plan and section views.

1. Minimum Spacing Parallel to the Grain (a₁ = 7 d)  
   – This is the distance between the centres of two adjacent screws along a line parallel to the wood grain.  
   – It prevents timber splitting and ensures full withdrawal strength when the screws are loaded axially (tension or compression).

2. Minimum Spacing Perpendicular to the Grain (a₂ = 5 d)  
   – The centre-to-centre distance between screws along a line perpendicular to the grain.  
   – It controls the stress field overlap in shear perpendicular to grain and avoids shear‐failure interactions.

3. Minimum End Distance (a₁,CG = 10 d)  
   – The distance from the centre of the threaded portion of the screw to the loaded end face of the member.  
   – Ensures sufficient timber embedment to develop full withdrawal and tensile capacity without end‐grain splitting.

4. Minimum Edge Distance on the Loaded Side (a₂,CG = 7 d)  
   – The offset from the screw centre to the nearest loaded side edge of the member.  
   – Prevents premature tearing out of fibres under lateral loads or combined axial plus lateral actions.

5. Minimum Edge Distance on the Unloaded Side (a₃,CG = 5 d)  
   – The distance from the screw centre to the unloaded (free) edge of the timber.  
   – Guards against local crushing and tear‐out when screws are driven in or under service loads.

Key to Figure 8.11a  
– “1” marks the centre of gravity of the threaded part of the screw within the timber.  
– Diagrams show both plan and sectional views, with arrows denoting the a₁ and a₂ spacings laid out at various angles α to the grain.  
– a₁,CG, a₂,CG and a₃,CG dimensions are always measured from point 1.

Contextual Notes (for verification of resistance)  
– These spacings and distances support the verification of all relevant failure modes of axially loaded screws: withdrawal of the threaded shank, head pull-through, head tear-off (when used with steel plates), tensile yielding or buckling of the shank, and block or plug shear when screws act in groups against a steel plate.  
– The minimum penetration length of the threaded part into the timber (on the “point‐side”) must be at least 6 d to develop full embedment strength.  
– For screws complying with EN 14592 (d = 6–12 mm, 0.6 ≤ d₁/d ≤ 0.75), characteristic withdrawal and tensile capacities are determined per EN 14592, and the effective number of screws (n_ef) may be reduced for parallel-to-shank loading (n_ef = 0.9 n).  
– All spacing provisions equally apply when screws are arranged at an angle α to the grain; the same dimension multiples (7 d and 5 d) are measured along the projected directions shown in Figure 8.11a.

(7) The characteristic tensile resistance of the connection (head tear-off or tensile capacity of shank), Ft,Rk, should be taken as:. F t,Rk = n ef f tens,k. where. is the characteristic tensile capacity of the screw determined in accordance with EN 14592;. nef is the effective number of screws, see 8.7.2(8)..
 (8) For a connection with a group of screws loaded by a force component parallel to the shank, the effective number of screws is given by:
 efn n= 0,9
 where:
 nef is the effective number of screws;

The table reproduced below (Table 8.6) specifies the minimum centre-to-centre spacings and the minimum distances from any screw to a member edge (“edge distances”) for axially loaded wood-to-wood or wood-to-steel connections. All dimensions are expressed as multiples of the screw’s outer thread diameter, d, and apply when the timber thickness t is at least 12 d (see clause 8.11a and EN 1995-1-1). These geometric limits are fundamental inputs to the verification of all relevant failure modes (withdrawal, head pull-through, head tear-off, tensile failure, buckling, block shear and plug shear) listed in paragraph (1) of the revised text.

Table 8.6 – Minimum spacings and edge distances for axially loaded screws  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------–  
| Screws driven               | Minimum spacing | Minimum edge distance |  
| ———————————————— | ———————————— | ———————————————— |  
| At right angle to the grain | 4 d             | 4 d                   |  
| In end grain                | 4 d             | 2.5 d                 |  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------–

Key points of the table and its context:

1. Scope and applicability  
   • Applies to screws loaded purely in axial tension or compression.  
   • Timber member thickness t must satisfy t ≥ 12 d; otherwise special detailing or alternative values are required.  
   • Minimum penetration length of the threaded part into the timber (“point-side penetration”) must be at least 6 d (paragraph 3).

2. Definitions  
   • Minimum spacing (centre-to-centre): the least allowable distance between adjacent screws, measured parallel to the grain or along end grain, ensuring that the withdrawal capacity of each screw is not reduced by overlapping stress cones.  
   • Minimum edge distance: the distance from the screw centre to the nearest free edge of the timber member. It prevents premature splitting under service loads.

3. Grain orientation cases  
   – At right angle to the grain (“side grain”): uniform demand on timber bearing strength and withdrawal resistance leads to both spacing and edge distances equal to 4 d.  
   – In end grain: although withdrawal resistance remains governed by similar embedment mechanics (hence spacing still 4 d), the edge distance is relaxed to 2.5 d because end-grain failure modes are less sensitive to splitting, but still require sufficient timber cover to mobilize pull-through and withdrawal strength.

4. Relationship to failure-mode verification  
   • Withdrawal failure (ax,α,Rk) and associated characteristic strengths f ax,α,k are calculated per clause 8.7 and formulae (8.38)–(8.40).  
   • Ensuring these geometrical limits prevents brittle splitting around screws and allows the designer to assume independent load-carrying capacity for each fastener up to the effective group size nef (paragraph 8).  
   • The table’s values feed directly into the determination of the effective number of screws (nef = 0.9 n for parallel-shank loading) and the characteristic tensile resistance Ft,Rk = nef·f tens,k (paragraph 7).

In practice, Table 8.6 is one of the first checks during layout design: you position fasteners so that neither withdrawal capacity nor edge-splitting issues compromise the assumed characteristic resistances in subsequent structural calculations.

The input is extracted from “Table 8.8 – Minimum spacings and edge and end distances for toothed-plate connectors types C1 to C9.”  It defines, for a range of connector orientations relative to the wood grain, the minimum centre-to-centre spacings (a-values) or clearances from edges and ends, expressed as multiples of dc, the characteristic connector size.  The six distinct spacing types, their applicable angle ranges (α, the acute or obtuse angle between load direction and grain), and the formulae for the required minimum distances are summarized below.

1. Spacing a₁ (parallel to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360° (all orientations)  
   – Minimum spacing: (1.2 + 0.3 |cos α|) dc  

2. Spacing a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum spacing: 1.2 dc  

3. Spacing a₃,ₜ (loaded end distance)  
   – Angle range: –90° ≤ α ≤ 90° (load directed toward the “end” face)  
   – Minimum spacing: 2.0 dc  

4. Spacing a₃,₆ (unloaded end distance)  
   This spacing applies when the load direction lies in the “unloaded” half of the end face.  It is defined piecewise over three α-intervals:  
   – 90° ≤ α < 150° and 210° ≤ α ≤ 270°  
       Minimum spacing: (0.9 + 0.6 |sin α|) dc  
   – 150° ≤ α < 210°  
       Minimum spacing: 1.2 dc  

5. Spacing a₄,ₜ (loaded edge distance)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 180° (load directed toward the “loaded” edge)  
   – Minimum spacing: (0.6 + 0.2 |sin α|) dc  

6. Spacing a₄,₆ (unloaded edge distance)  
   – Angle range: 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum spacing: 0.6 dc  

Key definitions and notes:  
• dc (in mm) is the reference connector dimension:  
   – For types C1, C2, C6, C7, C10 and C11: the nominal diameter.  
   – For C5, C8 and C9: the side length of the rectangular plate.  
   – For C3 and C4: the geometric mean of the two side lengths (√(l₁·l₂)).  
• α is measured in the horizontal plane between the load direction and the grain direction (grain = 0°).  
• All spacing values refer to centre-to-centre distances (for adjacent connectors) or clear distances to the timber member’s free edges/ends, whichever is critical.  

By applying these formulae, designers ensure that connector teeth have sufficient timber bearing between each other and to the member boundaries, accommodating changes in load orientation.

The table reproduced here (Table 8.9) specifies the minimum centre-to-centre spacings and the minimum edge- and end-distances for toothed-plate connectors of types C10 and C11. All distances are expressed in terms of dc, the characteristic connector size (diameter for circular-shank connectors, side length or geometric mean of sides for non-circular types). The three columns and six rows of the table break down as follows:

1. Column headings  
   ­– “Spacings and edge/end distances (see Figure 8.7)” lists the six distinct spacing or edge/end-distance parameters, a₁ through a₄,c.  
   ­– “Angle to grain” gives the range of fibre-direction angles α (in degrees) over which each spacing rule applies.  
   ­– “Minimum spacings and edge/end distances” provides either a fixed multiple of dc or an α-dependent formula (with absolute-value operators) that must be multiplied by dc.

2. Row-by-row description  

   a₁ (parallel to grain)  
     • Angle α: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360° (i.e. for all directions, since this spacing is parallel to grain)  
     • Minimum spacing: (1.2 + 0.8 |cos α|) dc  
       – This expression ensures extra spacing when the connector axis aligns with the grain, tapering off as the angle deviates.  

   a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
     • Angle α: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
     • Minimum spacing: 1.2 dc  
       – A constant spacing suffices because this distance runs across the grain.  

   a₃,t (loaded end distance)  
     • Angle α: –90° ≤ α ≤ 90° (i.e. connector axis within ± 90° of the grain direction on the loaded end)  
     • Minimum: 2.0 dc  

   a₃,c (unloaded end distance)  
     • Split into three angle intervals:  
       – 90° ≤ α ≤ 150°: (0.4 + 1.6 |sin α|) dc  
       – 150° < α < 210°: 1.2 dc  
       – 210° ≤ α ≤ 270°: (0.4 + 1.6 |sin α|) dc  
     • This captures greater required distances when the connector is oriented near perpendicular to the grain, relaxing in the mid-range.  

   a₄,t (loaded edge distance)  
     • Angle α: 0° ≤ α ≤ 180° (i.e. on the loaded edge side)  
     • Minimum: (0.6 + 0.2 |sin α|) dc  

   a₄,c (unloaded edge distance)  
     • Angle α: 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
     • Minimum: 0.6 dc  

3. Notes and context  
   – dc is defined in the surrounding clauses (for C10/C11, it is the connector’s circular-shank diameter).  
   – All formulae use absolute values of trigonometric functions to ensure symmetry about the principal fibre directions.  
   – These minimum clearances are mandatory to prevent wood splitting and to achieve the design characteristic load-carrying capacities (see 8.9(1)–(4) in the referenced standard).  
   – The user must refer to Figure 8.7 for the geometric definitions of a₁–a₄, and to clauses 8.9 and 10.4.3 for bolt-connector interaction rules.

The input “table” is in fact the multilingual title block of EN 1995-1-1 (Eurocode 5, Part 1-1) as it appears in the corrigendum. It is laid out in two side-by-side cells, one in French and one in German, each cell containing the full official title broken across several lines. Below is a reconstruction and detailed description of its structure and contents:

1. Table structure  
   • Two columns, no visible gridlines or rule—each column holds one language version of the standard’s title.  
   • Each cell uses internal line‐breaks and hyphens to limit line width.

The image is a schematic, labeled “Figure 9.8 – Determination of equivalent vertical action qᵢ and reaction forces from vertical and horizontal actions,” showing a rigid‐body representation of a two‐panel timber wall. The wall is drawn as two adjacent rectangles side by side, each outlined by a thick continuous line. A pair of vertical dashed lines inside the outer frame mark the boundary between the two panels.

Above the top edge of the panels a series of uniform downward arrows illustrate the equivalent distributed load qᵢ. In the center of the top edge a single, larger downward arrow denotes the concentrated vertical action Fᵢ,vert,Ed acting at a horizontal distance a from the left (leeward) corner. The arrowhead of Fᵢ,vert,Ed touches the mid-section of the right panel’s top edge; the dimension a is shown by a two‐headed horizontal arrow from the left boundary of the overall wall to the vertical line of action of Fᵢ,vert,Ed.

On the right face of the right‐hand panel, at mid‐height, a horizontal arrow pointing inward (from right to left) is labeled Fᵢ,v,Ed, representing the racking (in-plane shear) force. On the left face of the left‐hand panel at mid-height, a matching horizontal arrow pointing inward (from left to right) is also labeled Fᵢ,v,Ed, indicating symmetric shear action when panels are considered in combination.

Along the bottom edge, two sets of vertical reaction arrows appear at the panel corners. At the left bottom corner two upward arrows are labeled Fᵢ,c,Ed (the compressive edge reaction) and Fᵢ,q,Ed (the share of the equivalent distributed load taken at that support). At the right bottom corner two upward arrows are labeled Fᵢ,t,Ed (the tensile edge reaction) and Fᵢ,q,Ed. Between those bottom supports, a dimension bᵢ is marked by a double‐headed horizontal arrow spanning from the left to the right support, indicating the total length of the wall.

Beneath the figure is the formula qᵢ = (2 a Fᵢ,vert,Ed) / (bᵢ)², together with the definitions:
• a is the horizontal distance from the applied vertical force F to the leeward corner of the wall.  
• bᵢ is the total length of the wall.

Overall, the diagram translates a concentrated vertical load and an in-plane shear force on a rigid wall into an equivalent uniform vertical load plus support reactions, showing how overturning moments from horizontal and vertical actions are resisted by compression and tension at the base corners.

sections: 9.2.4.3  Simplified analysis of wall diaphragms – Method B

content:
The figure consists of two schematic line‐drawings, each showing a single straight member (e.g. a beam or column) loaded in axial compression and laterally braced at discrete points.  Both diagrams use the following conventions:  
- The member is represented by a heavy horizontal line.  
- Pin supports at the member ends are shown as small solid triangles beneath the line.  
- Axial compression forces N are indicated by thick arrows pushing inward on each end of the member.  
- Intermediate lateral supports (braces) are sketched as zig-zag “spring” symbols attached downward to the member and labeled “C.”  
- A horizontal dimension arrow (“a”) denotes the clear spacing between successive bracing points (or between a bracing point and an end support).  
- Each drawing is accompanied by a label “m = …” to indicate the number of equal‐length segments (span subdivisions) created by the bracing arrangement.  

1. Top Diagram (m = 2)  
  - Two-pin supports at the left and right ends carry axial loads N directed toward the member’s center.  
  - A single intermediate lateral brace (C) is placed at mid-span.  
  - A dimension line labeled “a” spans from the left pinned support to the central brace; implicitly, the distance from the brace to the right support is the same (so that the member is divided into two equal segments, hence m = 2).  
  - This arrangement illustrates the simplest case of one lateral restraint at the centroid of the member, halving the unsupported length.  

2. Bottom Diagram (m = 4)  
  - Again, pin supports at both ends resist the compressive end loads N.  
  - Three equally spaced intermediate braces (each labeled C) are attached along the member.  
  - A single dimension arrow “a” is drawn between the left-hand pin and the first brace; by symmetry the remaining inter-brace and brace-to-end distances are also each a, yielding four equal segments.  
  - Because there are now four panels of length a between supports, the label “m = 4” appears at the right of the member.  

Caption (beneath both):  
“Figure 9.9 – Examples of single members in compression braced by lateral supports.”  

Contextual note (from the Eurocode 5 corrigendum):  
– The variable “a” represents the overall span of the stabilizing system, in meters.  
– The integer m equals the number of segments (i.e. spans of length a) created by the bracing pattern.  
– These illustrations serve to define the parameters needed when calculating the design stabilizing (buckling-resisting) force FB,d for columns or beams with lateral restraints at discrete points (see 9.2.5.2).

sections: 9.2.4.3  Simplified analysis of wall diaphragms – Method B

content:
The illustration, titled “Figure 9.10 – Beam or truss system requiring lateral supports,” is a schematic line-drawing showing how a slender compression member (either a beam or a truss) is laterally braced to prevent buckling under combined loading and geometric imperfections.  The main features are as follows:

1. Overall Geometry  
- Two parallel, slightly bowed vertical members represent the beam or truss under second-order (P-Δ) effects.  Their curvature indicates the initial deflection due to imperfections; the mid-height point is marked “B” and the lower node “A.”  
- The total clear distance between successive braces is labeled “ℓ,” defined in the adjoining text as the overall span of the stabilizing system in meters.  

2. Attachment Points and Spacing  
- Three identical bracing connections are shown along the length of the member.  They are equally spaced by a vertical distance “a” between them.  These denote the points at which lateral bracing members tie into the main compression element.  

3. Bracing Element and Loads  
- To the right of the compression member is a solid rectangular block labeled (2), signifying the bracing assembly.  
- On the far right of this block is a uniformly distributed horizontal load, drawn as a dense field of small arrows pointing toward the bracing.  This is numbered (5) and corresponds to “External load on bracing” (for example, wind pressure).  
- At the base of that bracing block, a pair of horizontal arrows labelled (6) represent the “Reaction forces of bracing due to external loads” that the bracing transfers back into its supports.  

4. Transfer of Stabilizing Forces  
- Between the bracing block and the compression member are three large arrows (numbered (4)) pointing back into the member.  These signify the “Stabilizing forces” applied at the brace-connection points.  The braces oppose lateral displacement by pushing or pulling on the member.  
- On the far left of the main member, opposing arrows numbered (7) indicate the “Reaction forces of the truss system due to stabilizing forces.”  These return forces act on the main supports of the beam/truss.  
- At each brace-attachment level along the member, the axial compressive force “N” is shown at the foot of the member, highlighting that the member is under compression at those points.  

5. Key and Notes  
Beneath the diagram, a keyed legend lists:  
(1) n members of the truss system  
(2) Bracing  
(3) Deflection due to imperfections and second-order effects  
(4) Stabilizing forces  
(5) External load on bracing  
(6) Reaction forces of bracing due to external loads  
(7) Reaction forces of truss system due to stabilizing forces  

Above the graphic, brief text defines ℓ (overall span of the stabilizing system, in m) and kf,3 (a modification factor). This figure illustrates the arrangement and load-path for lateral supports as required by clause 9.2.5.2(3) in Eurocode 5 (EN 1995-1-1:2004) for determining the design stabilizing force on a rectangular beam’s compressive edge.

sections: 9.2.4.3  Simplified analysis of wall diaphragms – Method B

content:
The input table, labeled “Table 9.2 – Recommended values of modification factors,” appears in the context of Eurocode 5’s rules for determining stabilizing and deflection-related forces in timber-based wall and bracing systems (see clauses 9.2.5.3 and 9.2.5.2(3)). This table provides guidance on four distinct dimensionless coefficients (“modification factors”) that account for workmanship quality, span effects, material variation and other national or practical considerations. Their numerical ranges are intended for use in the calculation formulae scattered through clauses 9.2.4.3.1 to 9.2.5.3, notably in expressions (9.29), (9.30) and (9.35). National documents may choose specific values within these ranges, and the values underlined in the official standard represent the “recommended” default.

1. Table structure  
   - Two columns:  
     • “Modification factor” – the symbol used in the Eurocode equations, namely k_s, k_f,1, k_f,2 and k_f,3.  
     • “Range” – the minimum and maximum values between which each factor may be selected.

2. Rows and factor descriptions  
   1. k_s  
      • Range: 4 to 1  
      • Role: Accounts for the stiffness or stability of lateral bracing (clause 9.2.5.3(1) note). It modifies the effective deflection of the bracing system under horizontal loads (e.g. wind). A lower k_s (closer to 1) implies higher confidence in bracing stiffness; a higher k_s (up to 4) reflects more conservative assumptions on flexibility.  
   2. k_f,1  
      • Range: 50 to 80  
      • Role: Modification factor for solid timber elements in the calculation of the design stabilizing force F_B,d (see equation 9.35). It adjusts the compressive resistance at supports to account for potential geometric imperfections and workmanship variations.  
   3. k_f,2  
      • Range: 80 to 100  
      • Role: Modification factor for glued-laminated timber and laminated veneer lumber (LVL) in the same stabilizing-force formula (9.35). Because these engineered products have more uniform properties, their recommended k_f,2 values lie at the upper end of the scale, reflecting greater reliability.  
   4. k_f,3  
      • Range: 30 to 80  
      • Role: Applies specifically to the compressive edge of a rectangular beam (see clause 9.2.5.2(3)), modifying the computed stabilizing force on that edge based on overall span and quality considerations.

3. Use in design  
   • The values chosen for k_s, k_f,1, k_f,2 and k_f,3 directly influence:  
     – The design racking strength of walls and wall assemblies (through k_s in equations 9.29–9.30).  
     – The design stabilizing forces at wall footings or beam edges (through k_f,1, k_f,2 in 9.35 and k_f,3 in 9.2.5.2(3)).  
   • Designers or National Annexes select a single value within each range. The underlined figures in the published Eurocode serve as the default recommendation in the absence of a national choice.  
   • Sensitivity to workmanship, span length and bracing configuration is captured by these factors; more exacting quality control or stiffer systems permit selection of the lower end of each range, leading to less conservative (higher) computed capacities.

By documenting these ranges and their intended application, Table 9.2 ensures a transparent, tunable approach to accounting for real-world variability in timber construction.

Below is a detailed, RAG-friendly description of its components, hierarchy and key metadata, including the user-supplied modification to paragraph (3).

1. Document Identification and Metadata

 In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.
 Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.
 For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.
 In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreementT 1 T between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products – CPD – and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).
 The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

 Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.
 The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes:
 – as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire ;
 – as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services ;
 – as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)
 The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative DocumentsT 2 T referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standardsT 3 T . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these technical specifications with the Eurocodes.

(1)P EN 1995 applies to the design of buildings and civil engineering works in timber (solid timber, sawn, planed or in pole form, glued laminated timber or wood-based structural products, e.g. LVL) or wood-based panels jointed together with adhesives or mechanical fasteners. It complies with the principles and requirements for the safety and serviceability of structures and the basis of design and verification given in EN 1990:2002.
 (2)P EN 1995 is only concerned with requirements for mechanical resistance, serviceability, durability and fire resistance of timber structures. Other requirements, e.g concerning thermal or sound insulation, are not considered.
 (3) EN 1995 is intended to be used in conjunction with:

Below is a structured, self-contained description of the input table and its place in a design code context. This text is suitable for indexing in a retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) store.

Title  
  Table 2.1 – Load-duration classes

Purpose and Context  
  • In structural design standards (for example Eurocode or similar), each action or load is not only characterized by its magnitude and spatial distribution but also by how long it acts on the structure over its design life.  
  • The table groups all possible actions into discrete “load-duration classes,” which directly influence the partial safety factors used for strength and stiffness verification as well as consideration of time-dependent effects (creep, shrinkage, relaxation).  
  • For variable (non-permanent) actions – such as live loads, wind, snow, temperature – the appropriate duration class is chosen by estimating the typical frequency and accumulated time that the load level applies during the life of the structure.

Table 2.1 Layout  
  Column 1: “Duration Class”  
     – Gives a concise name identifying the class of load based on its accumulated presence over time (e.g. Permanent, Long-term, Medium-term, Short-term).  
  Column 2: “Order of accumulated duration of characteristic load”  
     – Defines the rough time bands for each class, expressed as the total aggregate duration (not necessarily continuous) at the characteristic magnitude.  

Core Entries  
  1. Permanent loads  
     • Accumulated duration: more than 10 years  
     • Examples: self-weight of structure, fixed equipment, soil pressure  
  2. Long-term loads  
     • Accumulated duration: 6 months to 10 years  
     • Examples: sustained live loads in parking garages, long-term storage loads  
  3. Medium-term loads  
     • Accumulated duration: 1 week to 6 months  
     • Examples: office occupancy loads, seasonal temperature effects  
  4. Short-term loads  
     • Accumulated duration: less than one week  
     • Examples: concentrated loads during maintenance, short-duration thermal shock  

How to Use This Table  
  • In strength and stiffness checks, assign each action to one of these four classes.  
  • Apply duration-dependent partial factors (γF) as specified elsewhere in the code.  
  • For variable and climatic actions (wind, snow), national annexes may prescribe locally appropriate assignments and factors.  
  • Table 2.2 in the standard gives worked examples illustrating typical assignments for common loads.

By capturing both the name and time window for each class, Table 2.1 provides a clear mapping from real-world load behavior to the design parameters needed for reliable structural safety assessment.

The input “Table 2.2 – Examples of load-duration assignment” is a concise, two-column reference mapping five standard load-duration classes to representative loading scenarios. It is intended to illustrate how various actions (loads) on a structure should be categorized for strength and stiffness verification, in accordance with the principles outlined in the accompanying text. Below is a structured breakdown of its content and context:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns:  
     – Load-duration class  
     – Examples of loading  
   • Rows: five distinct classes, ordered from the longest to the shortest typical application period.  

2. Load-duration Classes and Examples  
   The table pairs each class name with one or more example loads that typify the expected duration profile. These examples serve as guidance for engineers assigning actions to design categories:  
   
   – Permanent  
     • Example: self-weight  
     • Characteristics: Loads that act continuously throughout the life of the structure (e.g., the structure’s own dead weight).  
   – Long-term  
     • Example: storage  
     • Characteristics: Relatively constant loads that persist over a substantial portion of service life, but may be removed or varied only infrequently (e.g., stored materials in a warehouse).  
   – Medium-term  
     • Examples: imposed floor load, snow  
     • Characteristics: Seasonal or repeated loads of intermediate duration, such as occupancy loading on floors or snow accumulations that remain for days to weeks.  
   – Short-term  
     • Examples: snow, wind  
     • Characteristics: Transient loads lasting hours to a few days, including typical wind gusts or short snowfall events. Note that snow appears in both medium- and short-term, reflecting national or climatic variability in its duration.  
   – Instantaneous  
     • Examples: wind, accidental load  
     • Characteristics: Very brief actions lasting seconds to minutes, such as peak gust wind pressures or accidental impacts.  

3. Context and Application Notes  
   – The classification aligns with the requirement that “actions shall be assigned to one of the load-duration classes given in Table 2.1 for strength and stiffness calculations.”  
   – Designers estimate the typical variation of variable actions over time to determine the appropriate class.  
   – Climatic loads (snow, wind) may be assigned differently in national annexes to reflect local weather patterns.  
   – The table serves as a companion to a more detailed list of partial safety factors, which are adjusted based on load duration.  

4. Usage in a RAG Vector Store  
   • Metadata fields to capture:  
     – table_id: “Table 2.2”  
     – topic: “Load-duration classification”  
     – columns: [“Load-duration class”, “Examples of loading”]  
     – rows: five entries as detailed above  
     – source_reference: relevant design code or standard (e.g., Eurocode 1)  
   • Embeddings should highlight the mapping relationship between duration classes and typical loads, aiding retrieval in queries about load categorization, partial factor selection, or structural action assignment.

The table entitled “Table 3.1 – Values of k_mod” is a comprehensive matrix of modification factors (k_mod) for structural timber under various combinations of service classes and load-duration classes.  It is arranged as follows:

1. Columns (Load-Duration Classes):
   - Permanent action
   - Long-term action
   - Medium-term action
   - Short-term action
   - Instantaneous action

2. Rows (Service Classes):
   - Service class 1
   - Service class 2
   - Service class 3

3. Subdivisions:
   Although laid out in a single multi-cell grid, the entries are grouped into several sub-tables, each corresponding to a different timber stress category (for example bending, tension parallel to grain, tension perpendicular to grain, compression parallel to grain, compression perpendicular to grain, shear, etc.).  Within each sub-table the same service-class headings recur, but the numerical values differ according to the stress mode and, in some cases, joint type or cross-section form.

4. Key numerical patterns:
   - For bending and tension‐parallel sub-tables (solid and finger-jointed timber), k_mod values typically run from 0.60 (permanent, SC 1) up to 1.10 (instantaneous, SC 1).  Service class 2 matches class 1, and class 3 values are reduced (e.g. 0.50 → 0.90).
   - In shear and compression categories, k_mod figures drop further (e.g. permanent action as low as 0.20 in SC 2), reflecting greater sensitivity to sustained loading.
   - Instantaneous action uniformly yields the highest k_mod (often 1.10 or 0.90 in poorer classes), while permanent action gives the lowest.
   - Some sub-tables omit service class 3 entirely, indicating that certain stress modes are only defined for classes 1 and 2.

5. Footnotes and applicability:
   (1) Timber members must comply with EN 14081-1; round cross-sections with EN 14544.  Strength classes are given in EN 338.  
   (2) The effect of member size on strength may be taken into account via factors defined elsewhere.  
   (3) For rectangular solid timber with characteristic density ρ_k ≤ 700 kg/m³, the reference dimension in bending or tension is 150 mm; for smaller sections a size-factor k_h (given in the same standard) applies.  
   (4) If timber is at or near fibre saturation and will dry under load, the deflection factor k_def from Table 3.2 is increased by 1.0.  
   (5) Finger joints are to comply with EN 385.

6. Usage guidance:
   - Select the appropriate sub-table for the timber stress mode.
   - Read across the row corresponding to the service class (1, 2 or 3).
   - Identify the column for the anticipated load-duration (from permanent through instantaneous).
   - Apply the listed k_mod to characteristic strength values (for bending f_m,k, tension f_t,0,k, shear, compression, etc.) to obtain design values.

By capturing all load-duration scenarios across environmental service classes and timber stress modes, Table 3.1 provides the designer with a single reference for adjusting characteristic strengths in accordance with Eurocode 5 principles.

The input is an extract from Eurocode 5 (EN 1995-1-1), Table 3.2, which tabulates recommended values of the creep (deflection) factor k_def for a wide range of solid and engineered wood products. The factor k_def is used to account for long-term deformation under sustained loading in different service classes (i.e. varying moisture and temperature conditions). Below is a structured description of its contents and relevant contextual notes.

1. Purpose and Scope  
• k_def modifies short-term elastic deformations to predict long-term (creep) deflections.  
• Values are given for Service Class 1 (indoor, low humidity), Class 2 (intermediate humidity) and Class 3 (high humidity or permanent outdoor use) where applicable.  
• The table covers both solid sawn timber and a variety of wood-based panels, each referenced to their harmonised European standard.

2. Overall Layout  
• Column 1 “Material”: name of the timber or panel product.  
• Column 2 “Standard”: applicable EN or ENV reference for product specifications and characteristic properties.  
• Columns 3–5 “Service class”: k_def values for Service Classes 1, 2 and 3. A dash “–” indicates the product is not normally used or not assigned a value in that class.

3. Solid and Engineered Structural Timber  
• Solid timber (EN 14081-1), glued-laminated timber (EN 14080) and cross-laminated timber (EN 14374, EN 14279) share identical k_def values:  
  – SC1: 0.60  
  – SC2: 0.80  
  – SC3: 2.00  
  These products are designed for structural applications where creep under humid or wet conditions (SC 3) is significantly higher.  

4. Plywood (EN 636)  
• Part 1 (softwood plywood): SC1 = 0.80; no values for SC2 or SC3 (not common).  
• Part 2 (tropical hardwood plywood): SC1 = 0.80; SC2 = 1.00; SC3 not assigned.  
• Part 3 (plywood for moisture-resistant or external use): SC1 = 0.80; SC2 = 1.00; SC3 = 2.50.

5. Oriented Strand Board (OSB) – EN 300  
• OSB/2 (interior load-bearing): SC1 = 2.25; SC2, 3 not used.  
• OSB/3 and OSB/4 (humid or exterior environments): SC1 = 1.50; SC2 = 2.25; SC3 not used.

6. Particleboard – EN 312  
• Part 4 (general purpose) and Part 5 (heavy-duty furniture): SC1 = 2.25; Part 5 SC2 = 3.00.  
• Part 6 (moisture-resistant): SC1 = 1.50; SC2, 3 not assigned.  
• Part 7 (exterior grade): SC1 = 1.50; SC2 = 2.25; SC3 not assigned.

7. Fiberboard (Hard, Medium, MDF) – EN 622 series  
• Hardboard (EN 622-2): HB.LA products SC1 = 2.25; HB.HLA1/HLA2 SC1 = 2.25, SC2 = 3.00.  
• Medium-density fiberboard (EN 622-3): MBH.LA1/LA2 SC1 = 3.00; MBH.HLS1/HLS2 SC1 = 3.00, SC2 = 4.00.  
• MDF (EN 622-5): MDF.LA SC1 = 2.25; MDF.HLS SC1 = 2.25, SC2 = 3.00.

8. Contextual Normative Notes (EN 1995-1-1 Clause 3.2.2.1)  
• Glued laminated timber must comply with EN 14080; characteristic strength and stiffness classes in EN 1194 (see annex D).  
• A size effect correction (k_B) applies to bending depth or tension width h < 600 mm:  
   k_B = min { (600/h)^0.2, 1.1 }  
• Large finger joints (ENV 387) are prohibited in Service Class 3 when grain direction changes at the joint.  
• Member size also affects tensile strength perpendicular to grain.

9. Practical Use  
• In design checks, multiply the short-term deflection by k_def to obtain the long-term deflection estimate.  
• Select the k_def row corresponding to the product’s service environment.  
• Apply size correction and other normative provisions as required before assigning final design values.

This table (labeled “Table 4.1 – Examples of minimum specifications for material protection against corrosion for fasteners (related to ISO 2081)”) gives a concise matrix of fastener types versus environmental “service classes,” indicating the least-acceptable corrosion protection or base material for each combination. It is intended to guide designers, specifiers and purchasers in selecting fasteners that will attain a reasonable service life without premature corrosion. The table is further explained by notes a and b, and is referenced by clause 2.3.1.3 in the parent standard.

1. Table Structure  
   - Two main axes:
     • Vertical: six categories of fasteners and steel plate connectors, defined by geometry or size  
     • Horizontal: three service classes (1, 2 and 3), corresponding to increasingly severe exposure conditions  
   - Cell entries specify either:
     – “None” (no special corrosion-resistant material or coating beyond the fastener’s base steel), or  
     – Fe/Zn 12c, Fe/Zn 25c (two grades of hot-dip zinc coating), or  
     – “Stainless steel”  

2. Fastener Categories (rows)  
   1. Nails and screws with diameter d ≤ 4 mm  
   2. Bolts, dowels, nails and screws with diameter d > 4 mm  
   3. Staples  
   4. Punched metal-plate fasteners and steel plates up to 3 mm thickness  
   5. Steel plates from 3 mm up to 5 mm thickness  
   6. Steel plates over 5 mm thickness  

3. Service Classes (columns)  
   • Class 1: Typically interior, low-humidity or otherwise non-aggressive environments  
   • Class 2: Moderate humidity or occasional condensation (e.g. sheltered outdoors, bathroom interiors)  
   • Class 3: High humidity, saline or industrial atmospheres, severe condensation  

4. Minimum Protection Requirements  
   – Class 1  
     • Most large fasteners (bolts, dowels, d > 4 mm) and thicker steel plates (>3 mm) may use uncoated steel (entry = “None”).  
     • Small fasteners (nails/screws d ≤ 4 mm) also may be uncoated.  
     • Staples and punched-plate fasteners up to 3 mm require Fe/Zn 12c zinc coating.  
   – Class 2  
     • Fe/Zn 12c is the baseline zinc coating for all categories except bolts/dowels/d > 4 mm (which may still use uncoated steel).  
   – Class 3  
     • In the most aggressive service class, staples and punched-plate fasteners must be stainless steel.  
     • Small/d ≤ 4 mm and larger fasteners require a heavier zinc coating (Fe/Zn 25c).  
     • Steel plates of any thickness also require Fe/Zn 25c in Class 3.  

5. Footnotes and Additional Context  
   a. If hot-dip zinc coating is used, Fe/Zn 12c corresponds to Z275 and Fe/Zn 25c to Z350 as defined in EN 10147.  
   b. In especially corrosive conditions (beyond Service Class 3), one should consider heavier coatings than Z350 or switch to stainless steel.  

6. Relation to Broader Requirements  
   – Paragraph (1) of the source standard mandates that all metal fasteners and structural connectors be inherently corrosion-resistant or adequately protected.  
   – Paragraph (2) points users to this table for “minimum corrosion protection or material specifications.”  
   – The designation “service classes” ties back to environmental severity criteria in section 2.3.1.3.  

Use in a RAG Vector Store  
• Metadata fields could include: fastener type, size bracket, service class, recommended minimum protection (material/coating), applicable standard references (ISO 2081, EN 10147).  
• A knowledge graph entry might link “Service Class 3” to both “saline environment” and “high humidity,” enabling retrieval of the appropriate minimum coating or stainless-steel requirement when querying for fasteners in coastal applications.  

This structured summary will allow a retrieval-augmented generation system to match user queries such as “What’s the minimum treatment for 5 mm thick steel plates in a coastal environment?” directly to the “Fe/Zn 25c” requirement, with footnote context available on demand.

The image is a line‐drawing schematic, labelled “Figure 5.1 – Examples of frame analysis model elements,” showing a simple single‐bay truss or roof‐frame resting on a horizontal beam.  It is annotated to illustrate how system lines, supports, bays, external and internal members, and fictitious beam elements are represented in a frame‐analysis model.  A keyed numbering system (1–6) identifies each element:

1. System line (1)  
   • Every member—both main (external) and secondary (internal)—has an internal “system line” drawn as a dash-dot line.  
   • For external members (the two sloping top chords and the bottom horizontal member), the system line exactly coincides with the true geometrical centre-line of the profile.  
   • For internal members (in this case the single vertical web member), the system line is shown within the cross-section but may not coincide with the member centre-line, indicating a possible eccentricity to be accounted for in analysis.

2. Support (2)  
   • The left end of the bottom horizontal member rests on a simple support, depicted as a filled gray rectangular block directly beneath the member’s end.  
   • This indicates where reaction forces will be applied in the structural model.

3. Bay (3)  
   • An arrowed dimension line runs along the sloping top‐chord from the left support up to the roof apex.  
   • This annotated length is labelled “(3) Bay,” defining the clear span or panel length used in the numerical model.

4. External member (4)  
   • The bottom horizontal beam and the two sloping members forming the roof pitch are each tagged with “(4) External member.”  
   • These are the primary load‐carrying elements of the truss ‑ they carry axial forces, bending moments, and must be modelled with their true centre-line system.

5. Internal member (5)  
   • A single vertical web member rising from the mid‐point of the bottom beam up to the roof apex is labelled “(5) Internal member.”  
   • Its system line is shown inside the profile but offset if needed; the label reminds the analyst to account for any eccentricity between the actual centre‐line and the system line when verifying strength.

6. Fictitious beam element (6)  
   • Although not heavily emphasised in the drawing, the key entry “(6) Fictitious beam element” refers to light or dashed overlay elements one would introduce where connections or support eccentricities need to be modelled.  
   • In practice, these fictitious beams or springs would be placed to coincide as closely as possible with the actual joint configuration, replicating rotational stiffness or eccentric support conditions.

Overall, the figure communicates that in a first‐order, linear elastic frame analysis:  
– All system lines must lie within the member profiles. External members’ system lines coincide with their centre‐lines; internal members’ offsets (eccentricities) must be included in strength checks.  
– Supports can be modelled as simple or pinned, with any necessary fictitious beam or spring elements introduced to capture eccentricities.  
– The “bay” dimension defines the clear span between supports or nodes.  
– By adhering to these conventions—correct system lines, support modelling, fictitious elements—a consistent structural model is achieved for accurate determination of member forces and moments.

(1)P Frame structures shall be analysed such that the deformations of the members and joints, the influence of support eccentricities and the stiffness of the supporting structure are taken into account in the determination of the member forces and moments, see Figure 5.1 for definitions of structure configurations and model elements.
 (2)P In a frame analysis, the system lines for all members shall lie within the member profile. For the main members, e.g. the external members of a truss, the system lines shall coincide with the member centre-line.
 (3)P If the system lines for internal members do not coincide with the centre lines, the influence of the eccentricity shall be taken into account in the strength verification of these members.
 (4) Fictitious beam elements and spring elements may be used to model eccentric connections or supports. The orientation of fictitious beam elements and the location of the spring elements should coincide as closely as possible with the actual joint configuration.
 (5) In a first order linear elastic analysis, the effect of initial deformations and induced deflections may be disregarded if taken into account by the strength verification of the member.
 (6) The frame analysis should be carried out using the appropriate values of member stiffness defined in 2.2.2. Fictitious beam elements should be assumed to have a stiffness corresponding to that of the actual connections.
 (7) Connections may be assumed to be rotationally stiff, if their deformation has no significant effect upon the distribution of member forces and moments. Otherwise, connections may be generally assumed to be rotationally pinned.
 (8) Translational slip at the joints may be disregarded for the strength verification unless it significantly affects the distribution of internal forces and moments.
 (9) Splice connections used in lattice structures may be modelled as rotationally stiff if the actual rotation under load would have no significant effect upon member forces. This requirement is fulfilled if one of the following conditions is satisfied:
 − The splice connection has a load-carrying capacity which corresponds to at least 1,5 times the combination of applied force and moment

(9) Splice connections used in lattice structures may be modelled as rotationally stiff if the actual rotation under load would have no significant effect upon member forces. This requirement is fulfilled if one of the following conditions is satisfied:. − The splice connection has a load-carrying capacity which corresponds to at least 1,5 times the combination of applied force and moment.
 − The splice connection has a load-carrying capacity which corresponds to at least the combination of applied force and moment, provided that the timber members are not subject to bending stresses which are greater than 0,3 times the member bending strength, and the assembly would be stable if all such connections acted as pins.

The image, labeled “Figure 5.2 – Geometry of support,” is a black-and-white side-elevation schematic illustrating the bearing arrangement of a triangulated roof truss on its support. It focuses on three main elements: the sloping upper chord of the truss, the bearing pad (or bearing block) attached to that chord, and the support beneath. Two vertical reference lines define the allowable support width, and two horizontal dimension arrows (a₁ and a₂) quantify the overall bearing length and the offset of the pad within it.

1. Upper chord  
   - Depicted as a single, solid line of considerable thickness, the chord slopes downward from left to right at an angle of roughly 15°–20°.  
   - The left end of the chord drops vertically, forming a right angle, while the right end is truncated by a short “zig-zag” or break symbol, indicating that the member continues beyond the drawing frame.

2. Bearing pad (padstone)  
   - Directly beneath the sloping chord is a small rectangular block, representing the bearing pad that transfers load from the truss to the support.  
   - The block is centered vertically under the chord; its top surface abuts the underside of the chord.  
   - The block’s length (in the horizontal direction) is less than the full span of the dashed support width, indicating that it must lie entirely within the allowable bearing zone.

3. Support symbol  
   - Below the rectangular pad is a square of roughly the same width, with diagonal lines forming an “X” inside. This convention denotes a generic support or bearing surface (e.g., masonry, concrete pad, or steel bearing).  
   - The top face of this square aligns flush with the bottom of the bearing pad.

4. Reference planes and dimensions  
   - Two thin, vertical dashed lines stand on either side of the support symbol:  
     • The left dashed line passes through the pad’s left face.  
     • The right dashed line passes through the pad’s right face.  
   - A horizontal dimension arrow marked “a₁” spans between these two dashed lines, indicating the total allowable bearing length (denoted in the accompanying text as the length aB₁B).  
   - A second, shorter horizontal dimension arrow labeled “a₂” lies entirely to the left of the pad block, extending from the left dashed line to the pad’s left vertical face. This represents the offset distance aB₂B, which must not exceed one-third of a₁ or 100 mm, whichever is greater.  
   - Both arrows terminate in arrowheads touching the respective vertical lines, with the arrow labels positioned just above the dimension lines for clarity.

5. Caption  
   - Centered directly beneath the drawing is the legend:  
     “Figure 5.2 – Geometry of support”

Overall, the schematic conveys the critical geometric requirement that the bearing pad lie fully within the support width (a₁) and maintain a limited eccentricity (a₂). It supports the accompanying structural rules: no re-entrant external angles, minimum truss dimensions relative to span and member depth, and proper alignment of bearing widths within specified offsets.

(1) A simplified analysis of fully triangulated trusses should comply with the following conditions: − there are no re-entrant angles in the external profile;
 − the bearing width is situated within the length aB1B, and the distance aB2B in Figure 5.2 is not greater than aB1B/3 or 100 mm, whichever is the greater; − the truss height is greater than 0,15 times the span and 10 times the maximum external member depth.
 (2) The axial forces in the members should be determined on the basis that every node is pin- jointed.
 (3) The bending moments in single-bay members should be determined on the basis that the end nodes are pin-jointed. Bending moments in members that are continuous over several bays should be determined on the basis that the member is a beam with a simple support at each node. The effect of deflection at the nodes and partial fixity at the connections should be taken into account by a reduction of 10 % of the moments at the inner supports of the member. The inner support moments should be used to calculate the span bending moments.
