Below is a structured, detailed description of the three-part illustration (Figure 5.3), showing how initial geometric imperfections—angle φ at the supports and sinusoidal curvature with maximum eccentricity e—are imposed on a nominal frame or arch for second-order (P-Δ) analysis. The nominal (ideal) geometry is rendered as a thin, dash-dot line, while the imperfect shape used in the analysis is shown as a thicker continuous line.

1. Subfigure (a): Simple single-span frame  
   • Geometry: Two vertical columns of height h support a single inclined beam of length ℓ, meeting at the apex with an interior angle α. Both column bases are fixed (symbolized by small horizontal lines at ground level).  
   • Initial imperfection: On each side, the beam-to-column angle is altered from α to (α – φ). The dashed outline shows the perfect (φ = 0) shape; the solid outline shows both columns leaning slightly inward so that the apex angle is reduced by φ on each side.  
   • Annotation: A double arrow along the sloping beam marks length ℓ; a vertical arrow at the column marks height h; an angle symbol at the column-beam junction labels α.

2. Subfigure (b): Symmetrical arch under uniform loading  
   • Geometry: A smooth, single-curve arch spanning between two fixed supports, subdivided virtually into two equal half-spans, each of length ℓ₁.  
   • Initial imperfection: A symmetric sinusoidal bowing is superimposed so that the mid-span rise is offset by e = 0.0025 · ℓ₁ relative to the perfect arch line.  
   • Annotation: Arrows at the supports point to the two equal half-lengths ℓ₁; a vertical callout from the dashed to solid curves at mid-span reads “0.0025 ℓ₁”.

3. Subfigure (c): Non-symmetrical arch under asymmetric loading  
   • Geometry: An arch comprised of two unequal spans, ℓ₁ on the left and ℓ₂ on the right, between fixed supports. The rises may differ, creating a nonsymmetric thrust line.  
   • Initial imperfection:  
     – Each half-span is given its own sine-wave deviation: e₁ = 0.0025 ℓ₁ on the left, e₂ = 0.0025 ℓ₂ on the right.  
     – Additionally, a vertical drift of 0.0025 h is applied at one support to simulate uneven settlement.  
     – The left-hand column-arch connection angle is increased to (α + φ), while the right-hand side is reduced to (α – φ), reflecting asymmetric angle misalignment.  
   • Annotation: Arrows show ℓ₁ and ℓ₂; callouts mark “0.0025 ℓ₁,” “0.0025 ℓ₂,” and “0.0025 h.”

Contextual notes (per clauses 5.2 and 5.1):  
- φ takes the value 0.005 rad (for h ≤ 5 m) or 0.005·(5/h) (for h > 5 m).  
- The maximum eccentricity e in each member span is taken as 0.0025 times that span length.  
These assumed imperfections allow a linear second-order analysis to capture the amplifying effect of deflection on internal forces and moments.

It is labeled “Figure 6.1 – Member Axes.”  The member is depicted as a long rectangular prism (constant cross-section) with its long dimension running horizontally from left to right.

   – A straight beam-shaped block, with its length greatly exceeding its depth and width, is shown in perspective so that three faces are visible:  
     • The near (front) face (rectangle) at the left end.  
     • The top face, sloping back and to the right.  
     • The side face, receding into the page toward the right.  

 • Principal axes  
   – On the near (front) face, two mutually perpendicular axes are drawn:  
     • z-axis: a vertical line rising from the top edge of the left face, arrow pointing upward, labeled “z.”  
     • y-axis: a horizontal line extending leftward from the mid-height of the left face, arrow pointing outward, labeled “y.”  
   – The third principal axis, the x-axis, runs along the member’s length:  
     • Shown as a dashed line tracing the centroidal axis inside the beam.  
     • An arrow at the right end of this dashed line points to the right and is labeled “x.”  

 • Direction of grain  
   – A separate arrow with the label “(1)” and the caption “direction of grain” is drawn along the length of the beam, slightly inset from the top edge, indicating that the wood grain runs parallel to the x-axis (the long direction of the member).  

 • Caption and key  
   – Beneath the drawing is a small key reading “Key: (1) direction of grain.”  
   – The figure title “Figure 6.1 – Member Axes” appears under the key.  

Overall, the image succinctly defines a rectangular timber member’s orientation in space, with:  
 • The x-axis aligned with the member’s length (and grain direction)

The provided image is a schematic side‐view (cross‐section) of a simply‐supported timber beam under transverse compressive load, labelled “Figure 6.2 – Beam on supports.” It is intended to illustrate how the contact length and edge‐distance influence the factor kBc,90 when a beam member is resting on supports (see Eurocode Clause 6.1 and expressions 6.4/6.5).

Key features of the drawing:

1. Beam Geometry  
   • A long, horizontal rectangular block represents the beam, with its depth (h) into the page (not shown) and width (b, into the screen).  
   • The beam is drawn in simple outline, without grain‐lines or texture, to emphasize its structural role.

2. Applied Load  
   • Along the top face of the beam are a series of small, evenly spaced, solid downward‐pointing arrows.  
   • These arrows indicate a distributed compressive action or uniform downward loading perpendicular to the grain.

3. Support Reactions  
   • Two discrete support regions are depicted beneath the beam: one near the left end, one near the right end.  
   • Each support is shown as a group of solid upward‐pointing arrows clustered over a small horizontal segment (the “contact length” ℓ).  
   • The support arrows imply full‐width contact (across b) but only over a length ℓ along the beam’s length.

4. Dimensional Labels  
   • Under the left support, two callouts appear:  
     – “a” (a small horizontal double‐headed arrow from the beam’s left extremity to the start of the support contact region). This is the edge‐distance from beam end to support.  
     – “ℓ” (a double‐headed arrow spanning exactly the width of the under‐support arrow cluster), denoting the contact length in millimetres.  
   • The right support shows only the ℓ label; no “a” is called out there (implying symmetry or that the right end‐distance is not under consideration in the left‐support formula).

5. Caption  
   • Below the drawing is the legend “Figure 6.2 – Beam on supports,” reinforcing its role in the code text.

How this ties into the code clauses:

– According to Clause 6.1 (2) and (3), when a beam member is supported at discrete points, kBc,90 may be increased above the baseline value (1.0) if certain geometry conditions are met.  
– Equation (6.4) applies for an end support where the distance “a” from the beam end to the support edge is ≤ h/3. In that case, kBc,90 is computed as a function of ℓ/h and a/h.  
– Equation (6.5) applies for internal supports (i.e. neither adjacent to a free end). Figure 6.2 visually defines the parameters ℓ (contact length) and a (end‐distance) used in those expressions.

Stylistically, the figure uses clean, unshaded line art with uniform arrow symbols to communicate load and reaction without extraneous detail. The simplicity focuses attention on the two critical dimensions—contact length ℓ and edge‐distance a—required for evaluating compressive stress distribution perpendicular to the grain.

The illustration is labeled “Figure 6.3 – Determination of effective lengths for a member with h/b ≤ 2,5, (a) and (b) continuous support, (c) discrete supports.”  It is composed of three main beam‐in‐support sketches (subfigures a, b and c), plus at the right a simple cross‐section view showing member width b and depth h.  All three main sketches share these conventions:  
• The timber member is shown in side elevation, its depth h vertical and its length horizontal.  A gray line beneath represents the support plane.  
• Compressive forces are indicated by arrow clusters acting on the top face (and in (c) also on the bottom face).  
• A pair of dashed lines, diverging from the loaded area at a slope of 1 vertical to 3 horizontal, illustrate the triangular stress‐dispersal zone down to the support.  

Subfigure (a):  
– A concentrated load of length ℓ is applied on the top face, located at the member end.  
– To the right of the load, the remaining member length is labeled ℓ₁.  
– The stress‐dispersal zone is shown by the two 1:3 lines extending downward and outward toward the support.  
– The “effective length” ℓ_eff is marked beneath the loaded area on the support, starting at the beginning of the loaded zone and extending rightward.  
– A dimension note indicates ℓ_eff ≥ ℓ₁/4.  
– A dimension bar at right confirms the restriction h ≤ 2,5 b.  

Subfigure (b):  
– Similar to (a), but the concentrated load of width ℓ is set back a distance a from the member end.  
– The remainder of the beam to the right of the load is ℓ₁.  
– The same 1:3 dispersal zone is shown, and the effective length ℓ_eff is again projected onto the support.  
– Two dimensional constraints are called out: ℓ_eff ≥ ℓ₁/4, and the loaded zone must lie at least a/2 from the end (marked “≥ a/2”).  
– The h ≤ 2,5 b limit is again noted at the right edge.  

Subfigure (c):  
– The beam is supported on two discrete supports (small rectangles beneath the member), one under the loaded region and one under the free span to the right.  
– Two identical concentrated loads of length ℓ act on the top surface inboard of each support, and one of the loads is mirrored as a downward force on the bottom face directly under it (indicating bi‐directional compression).  
– Two pairs of 1:3 dispersal lines (one for each load) cone down to their respective supports.  
– Between the two cones is a dashed horizontal centerline.  
– The dimension a locates the first load from the left end, with ℓ and ℓ₁ marked to the right.  
– The effective length ℓ_eff is again shown, and the note ℓ_eff ≥ ℓ₁/4 appears.  The h ≤ 2,5 b constraint also applies.  

Right‐hand cross‐section:  
– A simple rectangle with its horizontal side labeled b (width) and vertical side labeled h (depth).  

Overall, this figure graphically defines how to determine the “effective bearing length” ℓ_eff for members whose depth h does not exceed 2.5 times their width b, under various loading and support arrangements.  The 1:3 stress‐dispersal lines and the minimum‐length rules (ℓ_eff ≥ ℓ₁/4; distance from ends ≥ a/2) provide the basis for calculating the factor k_Bc,90B in compression‐perpendicular‐to‐grain design according to clause 6.1.

The image consists of two simplified three-dimensional sketches of a prismatic timber member, each showing the orientation of shear stresses relative to the wood grain. Both views are drawn in isometric perspective, with the front-left vertical face fully visible, the top face slanting away toward the back, and the right face partially hidden by a dashed outline that indicates continuity of the grain direction into the unseen portion of the beam. A stylized “Z” symbol is drawn on the hidden right face to reinforce the local coordinate or grain axis orientation.

Figure (a):  
• The grain of the timber runs longitudinally along the length of the beam, from back to front (into and out of the dashed outline), and is depicted by the dashed back-face outline extending left to right.  
• A horizontal arrow is drawn on the top surface, pointing diagonally from the back right toward the front left. This arrow represents the component of shear stress acting parallel to the grain direction.  
• On the front vertical face, a single large arrow points vertically upward, indicating the complementary shear stress component on that face.  
• Together these two arrows form a shear couple whose net effect is to generate shear sliding along planes that are parallel to the grain. This corresponds to the case “shear with a stress component parallel to the grain” referred to in Eurocode clause 6.1.7(1) and captured by the design inequality τ ≤ fv,d (Equation 6.13).

Figure (b):  
• Again the grain runs axially along the beam from back to front, shown by the dashed outlines on both back and right faces.  
• A horizontal arrow on the top surface now points straight to the right, while on the front face another arrow points straight up. These two orthogonal components lie entirely perpendicular to the grain direction.  
• This represents “rolling shear,” where both shearing stresses act across grain planes rather than along them. In Eurocode terms, the rolling shear strength f v,dB is approximately twice the tension strength perpendicular to grain (see the note under Equation 6.13).  
• The sketch illustrates that under these conditions the relevant shear planes “roll” between annual rings rather than split along them.

This visual support directly complements the Eurocode expressions (6.13) and the note on rolling shear, as well as guiding design decisions at supports and under torsion (see Equations 6.14 and 6.15 in clause 6.1.8).

The illustration, titled “Figure 6.9 – Double tapered (a), curved (b) and pitched cambered (c) beams with the fibre direction parallel to the lower edge of the beam,” is composed of three schematic side-views of cambered timber beams. In each subfigure, the central “Apex Zone” (labelled (1)) is cross-hatched to show the region over which certain stress-reduction or stress‐increase factors (e.g. kBm,α in Eurocode expressions 6.43, 6.45, 6.54) must be applied when bending stress has a component at an angle to the grain.

1. Subfigure (a) – Double-tapered beam  
   • Geometry: A straight beam whose depth tapers linearly from full depth at each end down to a minimum at mid-span, then up again symmetrically.  
   • Apex zone: A central block of length h_ap along the beam, straddling the point of minimum depth. Its total length equals h_ap, split equally (0.5 h_ap each side) about the mid-axis.  
   • Labels:  
     – h_ap: total height (depth) of the section at the apex (mid-span).  
     – α_ap: taper angle measured between the top fibre of the beam and the horizontal datum.  
     – Arrows indicate fibre direction parallel to the lower edge.  
   • Purpose: Defines the region in which the reduction factor k_Bm,α for bending at an angle is computed using the taper angle α_ap and section height h_ap (see Eq. 6.43).

2. Subfigure (b) – Curved beam  
   • Geometry: A beam curved in plan or elevation into an arc of constant radius. The central apex is the midpoint of the arc, with both ends returning tangent to the horizontal baseline.  
   • Apex zone: The curved segment over which the local section height equals h_ap and where the curvature radius is r = r_in + 0.5 h_ap. The inner radius r_in is measured to the inner edge of the cross-section, and the mid-thickness fibre path (dashed) follows the radius r.  
   • Labels:  
     – α_ap = 0: the “taper” angle at the apex is zero because the top fibre is horizontal.  
     – r_in: inner radius of curvature.  
     – h_ap: depth of section measured radially from outer to inner fibre at apex.  
     – t: local thickness measured normal to the neutral fibre (small arrow).  
   • Purpose: Illustrates how to position and size the apex zone in a purely curved member when applying stress expressions for curved beams (e.g. Eq. 6.45).

3. Subfigure (c) – Pitched, cambered beam  
   • Geometry: A cambered beam in which both ends are not only curved but also “pitched” up, so that the top fibre at each end slopes upward at an angle α_ap toward the horizontal, meeting at a crowned apex at mid-span.  
   • Apex zone: A central curved block of length approximately h_ap, defined similarly to (b) but with end fibres angled. The inner curvature radius is again r_in, with the mid-thickness path at r_in + 0.5 h_ap.  
   • Labels:  
     – α_ap: pitch angle of the top fibre relative to the horizontal at the ends of the apex zone.  
     – h_ap, r_in, t: same meanings as in (b).  
   • Purpose: Shows the combination of taper (pitch) and curvature, defining the apex zone for stress checks under combined bending and axial load (refer to Eq. 6.21–6.22 and the k_Bm,α factor in Eq. 6.43).

Key takeaway: In all three geometries the “Apex Zone” is the centrally located region—whether straight, curved, or pitched—over which special stress-angle reduction factors must be evaluated. The dimensions h_ap, α_ap and r_in as shown feed directly into the formulas in the surrounding code text (e.g. Eqs. 6.43, 6.45, 6.54) that adjust the design bending strength fBm,d and the bending stress σBm,α,d for fibre-angle effects.

The image is a two-part schematic (labelled “Figure 6.10”) illustrating how a straight bar with a single notch behaves under pure bending in two different stress‐state conditions at the notch root. Each subfigure is drawn in elevation (side view), with the beam’s longitudinal axis horizontal and the neutral axis (no‐stress axis) along the top edge of the member.

General layout common to both a) and b):  
• The beam is shown between two vertical dashed lines, which denote the region of interest (the span over which the bending moment M is applied and evaluated).  
• Above and below, two thin horizontal lines represent the upper and lower faces of the prismatic member in the un‐notched (constant thickness) regions.  
• At mid-height, the bottom edge of the beam exhibits a single symmetrical notch: a stepped reduction in cross section produced by a straight taper (a chamfer) that transitions from the original full depth to a smaller reduced depth.  
• The taper angle is expressed by a ratio: “1 : i,” where the vertical drop is 1 unit and the horizontal run is i units. A dimension arrow along the sloping face calls out the vertical height “1” and below it the horizontal distance “i.”  
• On each end outside the dashed lines, a bending moment M is applied. Curved arrows next to these end zones show the sign and sense of the applied bending moment.

Subfigure a) “with tensile stresses at the notch”:  
• The left‐hand curved arrow, positioned outside the left dashed line, arcs in a counterclockwise sense; on the right side it arcs clockwise. These rotations produce sagging bending, so the lower fiber of the beam (where the notch is located) is in tension.  
• As a result, the small fillet at the notch root on the lower edge carries a tensile stress concentration.  
• The slope of the chamfer is drawn relatively shallow, indicating a long taper length i. According to the accompanying text, if the taper ratio satisfies i ≥ 10 (i.e. not steeper than 1:10), the local stress concentration may be neglected for tensile bending.

Subfigure b) “with compressive stresses at the notch”:  
• The end moments are reversed in sign compared with a): the left‐hand arrow now shows clockwise rotation and the right‐hand arrow shows counterclockwise rotation. This creates hogging bending, putting the lower fiber and notch root into compression.  
• Under compressive bending at the notch, stress concentration effects are likewise considered negligible, regardless of taper steepness.  
• The schematic again shows a chamfer of slope 1:i, but no constraint on i is noted for compressive cases.

Caption (reproduced):  
“Figure 6.10 – Bending at a notch: a) with tensile stresses at the notch, b) with compressive stresses at the notch.”

Overall, this drawing supports the textual provision that stress‐concentration factors at notches can be disregarded under (1) axial tension/compression parallel to the grain, (2) tensile bending when the notch chamfer slope is gentle enough (i ≥ 10), and (3) all cases of compressive bending at the notch.

Figure 6.11 illustrates the geometry and key dimensions of an end-notched beam with a rectangular cross-section, where the wood grain runs essentially parallel to the member’s length. The notch at the support end reduces the vertical depth of the beam that actually carries shear, and all shear‐stress calculations at that support should be based on the effective (reduced) depth, hef. Two views are shown:

1. Subfigure (a): Detailed side elevation of an end-notched beam under transverse loads  
   • Overall beam depth (h): Measured from the top fiber of the beam to its original underside.  
   • Effective depth (hef): The remaining uncut vertical distance from the top fiber down to the bearing plane where the support reaction is applied. The small inset at left repeats this dimension for clarity.  
   • Notch depth (h – hef): The vertical cutout removed beneath the beam to create the support seating.  
   • Notch inclination i: Defined by the slope of the underside bevel, producing a triangular notch profile. This inclination is set so that the horizontal projection of the notch equals i (h – hef). Typical values of the notch angle α (where i = tan α) are:  
     – 4.5° for laminated veneer lumber (LVL)  
     – 5.0° for solid sawn timber  
     – 6.5° for glued‐laminated timber (glulam)  
   • Horizontal offset (x): The distance measured along the beam’s underside from the inside corner of the notch to the vertical line of action of the reaction force. This offset is used in calculating moment and shear‐stress distributions at the support.  
   • Applied loading: A series of downward arrows on the top surface represents point loads or a concentrated load zone near the end. These loads produce shear at the support that must be checked against allowable shear stresses using hef as the depth.  
   • Support reaction: A single upward arrow beneath the bearing plane indicates the reaction force transferred from the support to the beam.  

   In this view, the notch slope is clearly drawn: the underside of the beam angles upward from the support contact toward the uncut interior. The sloping face length is √[ i² (h – hef)² + (h – hef)² ], but only its projections i(h – hef) horizontally and (h – hef) vertically appear in the dimensioning.

2. Subfigure (b): Simplified representation  
   • Shows the same beam cross-section reduced to its effective depth hef only, resting on a generic support block.  
   • A single vertical arrow marks the reaction force, emphasizing that for shear checks at the notch, the beam can be treated as if it were only hef thick.  
   • All other geometric details are omitted for simplicity; the essential point is that only the uncut portion contributes to shear resistance at the support.

By using hef in place of the full depth h, design calculations account for the weakened shear section created by the notch. Verification steps include confirming the notch angle α matches the timber type and checking that x, the lever‐arm offset, is correctly measured from the notch corner to the reaction line. This ensures accurate determination of shear stresses and adequate support performance for end-notched timber beams.

Below is a detailed, stand-alone description of the provided diagram and its context, suitable for indexing in a RAG-enabled vector store:

Image overview  
– The illustration is a two-dimensional line chart titled “12 – System strength factor k_sys for laminated deck plates of solid timber or glued laminated members.” It plots how the system strength factor k_sys varies with the number of loaded laminations in a continuous timber deck or floor.

Axes  
– Horizontal axis (abscissa): “Number of loaded laminations,” labeled with integer tick marks from 1 through 10. Each tick corresponds to an additional parallel lamination participating in the load distribution system.  
– Vertical axis (ordinate): “k_sys,” the system strength factor, running from 1.0 at the bottom up to 1.2 at the top. Major horizontal gridlines appear at k_sys = 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2, with thinner intermediate gridlines providing fine gradations.

Curves and key  
– Two distinct curves are plotted, each starting at k_sys = 1.0 when only a single lamination is loaded:  
  • Curve 1 (dashed line): Represents lamination assemblies held together by mechanical fasteners (nailed or screwed). It rises gradually from k_sys = 1.0 at 1 lamination, reaching about k_sys = 1.05 at 4 laminations and k_sys = 1.08 at 6 laminations. Beyond six, it levels off, plateauing at k_sys = 1.10 for 8, 9, and 10 loaded laminations.  
  • Curve 2 (solid line): Represents laminations that are pre-stressed or glued together. It increases more steeply, attaining k_sys ≈ 1.10 by four laminations, k_sys ≈ 1.15 by six laminations, and peaking at the maximum value of k_sys = 1.20 once eight or more laminations share the load. From eight to ten laminations, the solid line remains flat at 1.20.

Caption and legend  
– Below the chart is a simple legend (key) identifying line styles:  
  1. Dashed line equals “Nailed or screwed laminations.”  
  2. Solid line equals “Laminations pre-stressed or glued together.”

– Underneath the key is the figure caption: “12 – System strength factor k_sys for laminated deck plates of solid timber or glued laminated members.”

Contextual notes (derived from accompanying text)  
– This factor k_sys applies when multiple, equally spaced timber members are laterally connected by a continuous load-distribution system. When that system reliably transfers loads among neighboring members over at least two spans, the nominal member strength can be multiplied by k_sys.  
– For short-term loads (e.g., wind, live loads), this system strength factor accounts for the beneficial interaction among laminations.  
– If continuous members (tiling battens, purlins, or panels) effectively transfer loads between adjacent roof trusses spaced up to 1.2 m apart, a full system factor of k_sys = 1.1 may be assumed for nailed assemblies.  
– For glued or pre-stressed laminated decks, designers should refer directly to this chart (Figure 6.12 in the source) to select the appropriate k_sys based on the number of laminations under load.

Key takeaways  
– Mechanically fastened laminations gain modest system strength, capping at 10 percent improvement (k_sys = 1.10).  
– Glued or pre-stressed laminations achieve greater composite action, topping out at 20 percent strength gain (k_sys = 1.20) once eight or more layers share the load.  
– The benefit curve flattens beyond six to eight layers, indicating diminishing returns from adding more laminations in terms of additional system strength.

(1) When several equally spaced similar members, components or assemblies are laterally connected by a continuous load distribution system, the member strength properties may be multiplied by a system strength factor kBsysB .
 (2) Provided the continuous load-distribution system is capable of transfering the loads from one member to the neighbouring members, the factor kBsysB should be 1,1.
 (3) The strength verification of the load distribution system should be carried out assuming the loads are of short-term duration.
 NOTE: For roof trusses with a maximum centre to centre distance of 1,2 m it may be assumed that tiling battens, purlins or panels can transfer the load to the neighbouring trusses provided that these load- distribution members are continuous over at least two spans, and any joints are staggered.
 (4) For laminated timber decks or floors the values of kBsysB given in Figure 6.12 should be used.

The table is headed “Table 7.1 – Values of Kser for fasteners and connectors in N/mm in timber-to-timber and wood-based panel-to-timber connections.” It defines the characteristic slip modulus Kser per shear plane per fastener under service load, as a function of the fastener or connector type, the mean density of the timber member(s), and geometric parameters (diameter or plate thickness). Key points of context:  

•  Kser refers to the slip modulus in N/mm. In EN 26891 the same property is denoted kBs.  
•  ρm is the mean density of the timber member (kg/m³). If two timber-based members have different mean densities ρm,1 and ρm,2, an equivalent ρm is calculated by the geometric mean:  
     ρm = √(ρm,1 · ρm,2)  
•  d is the diameter of dowels, bolts, screws or nails (mm). For toothed-plate and split-ring connectors, dc is the thickness of the steel plate or ring (see EN 13271).  
•  For steel-to-timber or concrete-to-timber joints, the tabulated Kser (based on the timber density) may be multiplied by 2.0.  

Structure of the table:  

1. Fasteners with pre-drilling (Dowels; Bolts with or without clearance; Screws; Nails with pre-drilling)  
   Kser = ρm^1.5 · d ⁄ 23  

   •  Footnote: “Bolts with or without clearance” – any clearance-related deformation must be added separately.  

2. Nails without pre-drilling  
   Kser = ρm^1.5 · d^0.8 ⁄ 30  

3. Staples (pre-drilling assumed)  
   Kser = ρm^1.5 · d^0.8 ⁄ 80  

4. Split-ring and shear-plate connectors type B (EN 912)  
   Kser = ρm · dc ⁄ 2  

   •  Split-ring connectors type A and shear-plate connectors type B share this expression.  

5. Toothed-plate connectors (EN 912), subdivided into two groups:  
   –  Connectors C1 to C9: Kser = 1.5 · ρm · dc ⁄ 4  
   –  Connectors C10 and C11: Kser = ρm · dc ⁄ 2  

By systematizing the slip modulus by fastener category, diameter (or plate thickness) and timber density, Table 7.1 provides all the parameters needed to predict the joint deformation under service loads. These expressions are suitable for use in design or numerical analyses of timber and wood-based panel connections when assembling a RAG vector store of joined‐member properties.

The figure depicts a simply supported beam of span ℓ, with its total deflection broken down into a sequence of component “curves” and annotated arrows.  It is labelled “Figure 7.1 – Components of deflection” and is intended to illustrate how the following symbols (defined in clause 2.2.3) relate to one another:

  • wBcB (precamber – if applied)  
  • wBinstB (instantaneous deflection under load)  
  • wBcreepB (additional creep deflection developing over time)  
  • wBfinB (final total deflection = instantaneous + creep)  
  • wBnet,finB (net final deflection below the reference chord)

Layout and elements:

  1. Supports and Reference Chord  
     - Two simple supports are shown as triangular pedestals, one at each end of the beam.  
     - A straight horizontal line drawn through the tops of these supports represents the unloaded, undeformed chord of the beam.  

  2. Precambers (wBcB)  
     - A lightly dashed curve above the reference line, gently arching upward.  
     - Labeled “wBcB,” this illustrates any precamber intentionally built into the beam to counteract subsequent sag.  

  3. Instantaneous Deflection (wBinstB)  
     - A solid or darker curve lying below the reference chord, symmetric about mid-span.  
     - Marked “wInst” at mid-span.  
     - A vertical two-headed arrow from the reference line down to this instantaneous curve at mid-span is labeled “wInst,” quantifying the deflection occurring immediately upon loading.  

  4. Creep Deflection (wBcreepB)  
     - A dashed curve located below the instantaneous deflected shape, showing further sag that develops over time under sustained load.  
     - Labeled “wCreep.”  
     - A vertical arrow between the instantaneous curve and the creep curve at mid-span marks the magnitude of creep deflection “wCreep.”  

  5. Final Deflected Shape (wBfinB)  
     - A heavier dashed line (or dash-dot) tracing the sum of instantaneous and creep deformations.  
     - It lies furthest below the reference chord.  

  6. Net Final Deflection (wBnet,finB)  
     - A larger vertical arrow drawn at mid-span, extending from the reference chord down to the final deflected shape.  
     - Labeled “wNet, fin,” this represents the total net deflection below the straight line between supports (i.e. wInst + wCreep, minus any precamber).  

  7. Span Dimension  
     - Below the beam, a horizontal double‐headed arrow spanning between the supports is marked “ℓ,” denoting the beam’s clear span.  

Overall, the drawing makes it clear that the beam’s net final deflection wNet, fin is the algebraic sum of (instantaneous + creep) minus any precamber, all measured from the original chord. The figure thus provides a visual breakdown of how each component contributes to the total sag of a loaded, creep-affected beam.

sections: 7.2  Limiting values for deflections of beams

content:
Table title  
“Table 7.2 – Examples of limiting values for deflections of beams”

Purpose  
This table provides indicative serviceability limits for beam deflections, expressed as fractions of the span length ℓ, for two common support conditions. It is intended to guide the choice of allowable deflection depending on whether only instantaneous effects, time-dependent (creep) effects, or the combined final deflection are being controlled. These limits correspond to definitions in clauses 2.2.3(5) and Figure 7.1, where:  
- w_inst is the instantaneous deflection under dead and imposed loads.  
- w_creep is the additional deflection due to creep.  
- w_fin is the total (final) deflection including long-term effects.  
- w_net,fin is the net final deflection below a straight line between supports, calculated as w_inst + w_creep – w_fin (section 2.2.3).  

Structure  
The table is divided into two rows—one for beams simply supported on two supports, and one for cantilever beams—and three columns for each deflection component of interest:

Column headings  
1. w_inst  
2. w_net,fin  
3. w_fin  

Each cell lists a recommended range of limiting values given as “ℓ/divisor to ℓ/divisor,” indicating the span ratios between most stringent and least stringent acceptable deflection.

Detailed contents  

1. Beams on two supports (simply supported):  
   - w_inst: ℓ/300 to ℓ/500  
     • The beam is allowed an instantaneous mid-span deflection from 1/500 ℓ (tighter) up to 1/300 ℓ (looser).  
   - w_net,fin: ℓ/250 to ℓ/350  
     • Net final deflection limit including creep but excluding any intentional precamber.  
   - w_fin: ℓ/150 to ℓ/300  
     • Total final (long-term) deflection limit, representing the sum of instantaneous and creep deflections.  

2. Cantilever beams:  
   - w_inst: ℓ/150 to ℓ/250  
     • Instantaneous deflection at the tip between 1/250 ℓ and 1/150 ℓ.  
   - w_net,fin: ℓ/125 to ℓ/175  
     • Net final (creep-inclusive) tip deflection limits for long-term serviceability.  
   - w_fin: ℓ/75 to ℓ/150  
     • Overall allowable long-term deflection, including both immediate and delayed effects.  

Context and application  
– The lower bound of each range corresponds to a more conservative (stiffer) design limit; the upper bound may suffice where deformation is less critical.  
– Users should select limits in accordance with the severity of serviceability requirements, occupant comfort, finishes, or alignment tolerances.  
– National choices and any adjustments to these recommended values are documented in the National Annex.  
– These values assume linear elastic behavior for instantaneous deflection; long-term deflections account for creep factors as per section 2.2.3.

1. Overall layout

The provided drawing, labeled “Figure 8.1 – Inclined force transmitted by a connection,” consists of two schematic views (a and b) illustrating how an angled fastener introduces both shear and splitting forces in a timber member. Below is a detailed verbal description of each part, together with how the annotated dimensions and forces relate to the EC5 provisions quoted in the accompanying text.

1. General arrangement  
- The connection consists of a single fastener (nail, bolt or punched metal plate) driven through a timber member at an inclination α to the grain.  
- The timber member has total height h and thickness b. The fastener’s penetration defines a loaded edge distance he, measured from the centre of the most distant fastener (or plate edge) to the bearing face.  

2. View (a) – Elevation of an inclined fastener in a single timber member  
- The fastener is shown as a rectangular rod or plate tilted upward at an angle α relative to the horizontal grain direction. Two small circles represent nail shank cross-sections (or bolt holes) on the plate’s face.  
- A vertical downward design shear force on the “left side” of the fastener is denoted Fv,Ed,1; on the “right side,” a comparable downward shear is Fv,Ed,2. These represent the two potential splitting planes in the timber, one on each side of the fastener.  
- The design axial tension in the fastener, resulting from the component of the overall applied force along the fastener axis, is shown by the upward-pointing arrow labeled FEd.  
- Perpendicular to the grain, the tension component is FEd·sin α, which tends to split the timber. The Eurocode requires that the maximum of the two shear demands Fv,Ed = max(Fv,Ed,1; Fv,Ed,2) does not exceed the design splitting capacity Fv,90,Rd.  

3. View (a) – Key dimensions and geometry  
- α: angle between fastener axis and timber grain (horizontal reference).  
- he: loaded edge distance from the fastener’s centreline to the loaded grain face.  
- h: total member height.  
- b: member thickness (in the out-of-page direction in (a), but shown more clearly in (b)).  

4. View (b) – Isometric or cross-section through two timber members joined by an inclined plate  
- Two timber elements are shown in offset, forming a lap joint. The punched metal plate fastener passes through both members at the same inclination α.  
- The plate’s width parallel to the grain is partitioned as b/2 into each member. This emphasizes that the effective splitting check must consider the loaded edge distance on each side of the plate.  
- The plate thickness corresponds to the member thickness b, indicating a snug fit through the joint.  

5. Relation to characteristic splitting capacity formula  
- For softwoods, the characteristic splitting capacity F90,Rk is given by  
   F90,Rk = 14 · w · b · he · (1 – he/h)  
   where w is a modification factor (≥1 for punched metal plates, =1 for other fasteners), b is plate or member thickness, he is loaded edge distance, and h is member height.  
- The design capacity Fv,90,Rd is then derived from F90,Rk with the appropriate partial safety factor according to clause 2.4.3 of the code.  

6. Splitting check criterion  
- The Eurocode requirement Fv,Ed ≤ Fv,90,Rd ensures that the perpendicular tension component does not exceed the timber’s ability to resist splitting along grain lines.  
- Because two potential splitting planes exist (either side of the fastener), the governing demand is the larger of Fv,Ed,1 and Fv,Ed,2.  

In summary, Figure 8.1 clearly communicates that an angled connection in timber induces both axial tension and shear in the fastener, which translates into a splitting demand on the wood. The dimensions α, he, b and h, together with the shear forces Fv,Ed,1 and Fv,Ed,2, feed directly into the Eurocode formulas (8.2–8.5) to determine whether the arrangement is safe against splitting perpendicular to the grain.

The image is a schematic set of eleven cross-sectional sketches (Figure 8.2) illustrating the principal failure modes of fasteners in timber and panel connections, under both single-shear and double-shear loading.  Each sketch is labelled by a lower-case letter (a–f for single shear, g–k for double shear) and shows two or three timber or panel elements (one or two shaded to distinguish the main “loaded” member), connected by a single fastener (nail, screw, bolt or dowel) drawn as a solid black rod.  Bold zig-zag lines or pinned‐hinge symbols superimposed on the timber represent the assumed failure surfaces or plastic hinge locations according to Johansen’s yield model or brittle embedment/splitting modes.

Top row: single shear (key: “(1) Single shear”), two elements of thickness t₁ (main member) and t₂ (side member) connected by one fastener passing horizontally through both layers.

  a) Ductile fastener yielding – plastic hinges form in the loaded timber member on either side of the fastener, with the fastener acting as a plastic hinge at the interface.  
  b) Ductile yielding in the side member only – hinges develop in the unshaded member.  
  c) Brittle embedment failure – a diagonal crack emanates from the fastener shank through the loaded member, at roughly a 45° grain angle.  
  d) Tensile splitting of the loaded member – the zig-zag line runs across its entire thickness, indicating a full-depth split.  
  e) Brittle embedment in the side member – a diagonal or shear plane through the shaded piece only.  
  f) Combined failure – a mix of embedment in one member and hinge formation or splitting in the other, indicated by a stepped fracture line.

Bottom row: double shear (key: “(2) Double shear”), three elements in series, outer members of thickness t₁ sandwiching a central member of thickness t₂.  The fastener passes through all three, and the annotated distances indicate t₁, t₂, and again t₁.

  g) Ductile yielding in both outer members – hinges form symmetrically on either side of the central piece.  
  h) Ductile yielding localized to one outer member – plastic hinges only in the left or right outer plank.  
  j) Brittle embedment failure – diagonal shear planes through the central panel plus one outer plank.  
  k) Full‐depth splitting across all three members – a continuous brittle fracture line spanning the entire sandwich.

Beneath the diagrams is a simple legend:  
  • (1) Single shear  
  • (2) Double shear

     • t₁: lesser of timber side thickness or penetration depth  
     • t₂: timber middle-member thickness  
     • d: fastener diameter  
     • Mᵧ,Rk: fastener yield moment  
     • Fₐₓ,Rk: withdrawal capacity of the fastener  

3. Failure‐mode illustrations (bottom)  
   Captioned “Figure 8.3 – Failure modes for steel-to-timber connections,” a row of nine simple line drawings labelled a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h and i/j l shows typical failure patterns:  
   - a) Bearing (embedment) in timber under single shear  
   - b) Fastener yield with tensile “rope effect”  
   - c) Timber splitting or crack along grain under load  
   - d) Group failure along fastener perimeter  
   - e) Bending of the fastener combined with embedment  
   - f) Double‐shear bending with a central steel plate (dimension t₁ indicated)  
   - g) Yield‐controlled failure in double shear  
   - h) Withdrawal or pull-out failure  
   - i/j l) Outer‐member bending scenarios with thin versus thick steel plates (t₂ dimension indicated)  

Overall, the page lays out a systematic method for selecting the governing expression for Fv,Rk based on plate thickness and shear‐plane configuration, then cross-references pictorial failure modes to help the engineer visualize how each limit state might occur in service.

The image consists of two simplified black-and-white line drawings, labeled “(a)” and “(b),” showing respectively a single shear connection and a double shear connection by means of a nail driven through timber members. Each drawing uses cross-hatching to indicate one timber element and plain white to indicate the others, with a single smooth nail (represented as a solid black circle head on the left feeding into a slender line) passing horizontally through the stack of members. Dimension arrows beneath each diagram mark the two thicknesses t₁ and t₂.

1. Single Shear Connection (figure a)  
   • There are two timber components in contact. The left-most member (unhatched) is the head-side timber; the right-most member (hatched) is the point-side timber.  
   • A single nail enters from the left, its head flush against the unhatched member, and exits into the hatched member without penetrating beyond it.  
   • Beneath this assembly are two horizontal dimension lines: the farther arrowed line underneath the unhatched piece is labeled t₁, and the nearer arrowed line beneath the hatched piece is labeled t₂. These denote head-side thickness (t₁) and point-side penetration (t₂) respectively.

2. Double Shear Connection (figure b)  
   • Three timber components are shown: two outer members (plain white) sandwiching one central member (cross-hatched). The central piece is slightly deeper in hatch-density to emphasize its role.  
   • A single nail enters from the left through the first outer member, passes through the central member completely, and exits into the second outer member on the right, but does not protrude beyond it on that side.  
   • Beneath, two arrow-dimension lines are reversed in order compared with (a): the longer arrow-to-arrow span covering the central (hatched) block is labeled t₂, and the shorter span under the right-hand outer member is labeled t₁. Here t₂ represents the central member thickness, while t₁ corresponds to the minimum of head-side timber thickness and point-side penetration in a double shear connection.

General visual features:  
- All timber members are drawn as simple rectangular blocks, with the central one in (b) further emphasized by heavier cross-hatching.  
- The nail is depicted by a filled black circle for the head, then a consistent thin line for the shank running straight through the members.  
- Dimension arrows are single-headed at each end, connected by a thin line, and annotated with “t₁” or “t₂” in a plain sans-serif font.

Below is a structured description of Table 8.1 (“Values of k_ef”) and its role in the design of nailed timber connections. This description is intended for ingestion into a RAG vector store and connects the table back to the surrounding commentary (clauses 8.1.2(4) and 8.17) on effective fastener numbers in a single nail row.

1. Purpose of k_ef  
   • In a single row of nails loaded parallel to the grain, the nominal load-carrying capacity must be reduced when the nails are too closely spaced.  
   • The reduction factor k_ef accounts for interaction between adjacent fasteners in the same row.  
   • The effective number of nails, n_ef, is then calculated as:  
        n_ef = n · k_ef  
     where n is the actual number of nails in that row (see clause 8.1.2(4) and equation 8.17).

2. Definition of “a”  
   • a = centre-to-centre spacing between nails, measured perpendicular to the grain direction.  
   • Expressed in multiples of the nail diameter d (so a = 2d, 3d, 4d, 5d, etc.).

3. Table 8.1: k_ef Values  
   The table splits values into two cases—“Not predrilled” and “Predrilled”—and lists k_ef for standard spacings a = 2d, 3d, 4d, and 5d:

   – a = 2d  
     • Not predrilled: k_ef = 1.0  
     • Predrilled:     k_ef = 1.0  

   – a = 3d  
     • Not predrilled: k_ef = 0.85  
     • Predrilled:     k_ef = 0.85  

   – a = 4d  
     • Not predrilled: k_ef = 0.70  
     • Predrilled:     k_ef = 0.70  

   – a = 5d  
     • Not predrilled: no value given (dash “–”)  
     • Predrilled:     k_ef = 0.50  

4. Footnote on Interpolation  
   • For any intermediate spacing between the tabulated values (e.g. a = 2.5d or 3.7d), linear interpolation of k_ef between the two nearest tabulated points is permitted.  
   • This allows a continuous reduction factor rather than abrupt jumps as spacing varies.

5. Practical Implications  
   • When nails are very close (2d apart), there is no reduction (k_ef = 1.0): they can be considered to act independently.  
   • As spacing increases to 3d and 4d, k_ef reduces to 0.85 and 0.70 respectively, reflecting some loss of individual capacity due to splitting risk and stress fields overlapping.  
   • For widely spaced nails (5d), only pre-drilled holes have a published reduction (k_ef = 0.5); non-predrilled nails at this spacing are not covered by this table and would require engineering judgement or reference to other clauses.

6. Connection Back to Clauses  
   • Clause 8.1.2(4) instructs that, in the absence of sufficient perpendicular staggering (at least 1d, see Figure 8.6), this k_ef must be applied to n when calculating the parallel-grain capacity of a nailed row.  
   • Equation 8.17 formalizes n_ef = n · k_ef, ensuring that designers do not overestimate the group capacity of closely spaced fasteners.  
   • Note also clause (9) which mandates at least two nails per connection—so n ≥ 2 before k_ef is invoked.

By capturing both the numerical values and their intended use—spacing definitions, pre-drill condition, interpolation allowance, and linkage to effective fastener count—this description fully contextualizes Table 8.1 for downstream retrieval and RAG-based reasoning.

Table 8.2 defines the minimum nail spacings and end-/edge-distances expressed as multiples of the nail diameter d. The required distance depends on  
• the angle α between the applied load and the grain direction,  
• the characteristic timber density ρₖ (two categories: ≤ 420 kg/m³, and 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³), and  
• whether the timber is pre-drilled.  

The table is organised into four parts, corresponding to the geometric arrangement of nails:  
1. Spacing of nails along a single row parallel to the grain.  
2. Spacing between parallel rows of nails (perpendicular to the grain).  
3. Distance from nails to timber ends (loaded or unloaded).  
4. Distance from nails to timber edges (loaded or unloaded).  

Definitions:  
– α: angle between the nail’s lateral load direction and the wood grain (0° = along grain, 90° = across grain).  
– d: nail diameter.  
– “Without predrilled holes” uses denser values; “with predrilled holes” permits reduced spacings.  

1. Spacing within one row (parallel to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°.  
   – For ρₖ ≤ 420 kg/m³:  
     • d < 5 mm: spacing ≥ (5 + 5 |cos α|) d  
     • d ≥ 5 mm: spacing ≥ (5 + 7 |cos α|) d  
   – For 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³: spacing ≥ (7 + 8 |cos α|) d  
   – With pre-drilled holes: spacing ≥ (4 + |cos α|) d  

2. Spacing of rows (perpendicular to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°.  
   – Without pre-drilling:  
     • ρₖ ≤ 420 kg/m³: spacing ≥ 5 d  
     • 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³: spacing ≥ 7 d  
   – With pre-drilled holes: spacing ≥ (3 + |sin α|) d  

3. End distances (nail to timber end)  
   – Two angle sectors:  
     a) –90° ≤ α ≤ 90° (force tipping toward one end)  
       • ρₖ ≤ 420 kg/m³: distance ≥ (10 + 5 cos α) d  
       • 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³: distance ≥ (15 + 5 cos α) d  
       • with pre-drilling: distance ≥ (7 + 5 cos α) d  
     b) 90° ≤ α ≤ 270° (force tipping toward the opposite end)  
       • ρₖ ≤ 420 kg/m³: distance ≥ 10 d  
       • 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³: distance ≥ 15 d  
       • with pre-drilling: distance ≥ 7 d  

4. Edge distances (nail to timber edge)  
   – Two angle sectors:  
     a) 0° ≤ α ≤ 180° (loaded edge facing the force)  
       • ρₖ ≤ 420 kg/m³:  
         – d < 5 mm: ≥ (5 + 2 sin α) d  
         – d ≥ 5 mm: ≥ (5 + 5 sin α) d  
       • 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³:  
         – d < 5 mm: ≥ (7 + 2 sin α) d  
         – d ≥ 5 mm: ≥ (7 + 5 sin α) d  
       • with pre-drilling:  
         – d < 5 mm: ≥ (3 + 2 sin α) d  
         – d ≥ 5 mm: ≥ (3 + 4 sin α) d  
     b) 180° ≤ α ≤ 360° (force toward the opposite edge)  
       • ρₖ ≤ 420 kg/m³: ≥ 5 d  
       • 420 < ρₖ ≤ 500 kg/m³: ≥ 7 d  
       • with pre-drilling: ≥ 3 d  

Notes on application (from clauses 8.3.1.2(1)–(7)):  
– Smooth nails require deeper penetration lengths (≥ 8 d in side grain, ≥ 6 d for other types).  
– Special rules apply for nails in end grain (secondary vs. primary structures, load-capacity reduction factors, minimum penetration of 10 d, service class restrictions).  
– Timber thinner than a critical thickness t (a function of d and ρₖ given by expressions 8.18 and 8.19) must be pre-drilled to avoid splitting.  

This structured breakdown allows a RAG vector store to index each geometric case (parallel spacing, row spacing, end distance, edge distance) by angle sector, density category, nail diameter threshold, and pre-drilling condition, linking back to the relevant clauses for context.

Figure 8.8 in the source standard presents two schematic cross-sectional views of a nail subjected to withdrawal (axial) loading when driven into timber: case (a) for nailing perpendicular to the grain, and case (b) for slant nailing. Each drawing is annotated with the key geometric quantities that enter the characteristic withdrawal capacity equations.

1. General layout  
   - In both subfigures, the top element is drawn as a solid rectangular “block” representing the member being pulled off, and the bottom element is the receiving member into which the nail is driven.  
   - A large upward-pointing arrow is drawn on the top block (indicating the tensile withdrawal force acting to pull the nail out), and a matching downward arrow is drawn on the bottom block (the reaction load).  

2. Subfigure (a): Nailing perpendicular to the grain  
   - A single straight nail of diameter d is shown running vertically through the top member and penetrating into the bottom member.  
   - The diameter of the nail is called out by a short leader line on the shank labeled “d.”  
   - Two double-headed dimension arrows appear on the right side of the figure:  
     • The shorter arrow between the underside of the top member and the top surface of the bottom member marks the embedment length of the nail in the receiving timber; this is labeled “t_pen” (penetration length).  
     • The longer arrow spanning the full thickness of the bottom member is labeled “t” (thickness of the bottom element).  
   - Together, these dimensions distinguish the total member thickness from the portion of that thickness actually used by the nail to resist withdrawal.  

3. Subfigure (b): Slant nailing  
   - Two identical nails are shown driven at equal but opposite angles (forming an “X” shape inside the lower element). This arrangement illustrates a typical paired, slanted nailing configuration.  
   - Each nail is inclined relative to the member surfaces at the same angle.  
   - On the right, the dimension “t” again marks the perpendicular thickness of the bottom member, measured vertically.  
   - A second double-headed arrow, drawn along the axis of one of the slanted nails, indicates the penetration length along the nail’s own line of action; this is also labeled “t_pen.”  
   - A small offset arrow along the slanted line shows the incremental distance between the nail axis and the face of the bottom member, used in calculating the effective embedment.  

4. Context and relevance  
   - These two configurations are referenced by clauses (4), (8.20), (8.21) and (8.22) of the standard as the geometries for which the characteristic withdrawal capacities (FBax,RkB) must be calculated.  
   - The standard specifies that smooth nails are excluded from long-term axial load resistance, only threaded portions of nails can carry axial tension, and nails seated into end grain are ineffective.  
   - For “nails other than smooth nails as defined in EN 14592,” one must determine FBax,RkB by evaluating both the perpendicular and slanted geometries and taking the smaller value.  

In summary, Figure 8.8 provides clear, annotated geometry for calculating the withdrawal strength of appropriately threaded nails in both perpendicular and slanted installations, defining the embedment length t_pen relative to the member thickness t and the nail diameter d.

The illustration is a schematic cross-sectional view of a U-shaped staple driven through two timber members, annotated to show all relevant geometrical parameters used for design checks in timber connections. The drawing is intended as “Figure 8.9 – Staple dimensions” and comprises the following elements:

1. Overall Geometry  
   • The staple has a straight, horizontal crown and two vertical legs of equal length.  
   • The two timber elements are shown as two horizontal blocks joined at a thin interface line. The crown of the staple bridges across the interface, while the legs penetrate into the lower member.

2. Centreline References  
   • A vertical dashed centerline passes through the midpoint of the crown, marked in the key as (1) “staple centre.”  
   • Horizontal dashed lines indicate the plane of the upper timber member’s lower face and the upper face of the lower timber member.

3. Dimension “b” – Crown Width  
   • Two opposing arrow-head dimension lines run horizontally from one outer edge of the staple crown to the other, labeled “b.”  
   • This distance measures the clear span of the crown (outside-to-outside of the legs) and is required to be at least six times the leg diameter d when designing staples to Eurocode rules.

4. Dimension “d” – Leg Diameter  
   • A short horizontal dimension line at the tip of one leg shows the distance between the outer edge of the leg and the outer edge of the opposite leg’s tip region, labeled “d.”  
   • For staples with non-circular cross-section, d is defined as the square root of the product of the two cross-sectional dimensions.

5. Penetration Depths  
   • t1: A vertical double-headed arrow between the crown plane (upper dashed timber face) and the join line (interface between the two timber members). This indicates the minimum embedment into the upper member, sometimes used for checking withdrawal capacity above the joint.  
   • t2: A longer vertical double-headed arrow from the crown plane down to the base of the lower timber block, representing the total penetration length of the legs below the crown. Eurocode requires t2 to be at least 14 d for staples with rectangular cross-section.

6. Key and Caption  
   • A small note at the bottom labels “(1) staple centre.”  
   • Below the drawing is the figure caption “Figure 8.9 – Staple dimensions.”

7. Graphical Style  
   • All structural outlines (staple and timber) are shown with bold black lines.  
   • Dimension lines are thin with filled arrowheads and textual labels in plain font.  
   • Dashed lines denote hidden or reference planes (centreline and timber faces).  
   • The interface between the two timber pieces is represented as a thin solid line across the width of the page.

Overall, this figure provides a clear, to-scale representation of the staple geometry—crown width b, leg diameter d, and penetration depths t1 and t2—needed to verify compliance with spacing, embedment, and load-carrying capacity provisions (including minimum crown-to-grain angles and staple spacing) as outlined in section 8.3.1.2 of the timber design standard.

The image is a black-and-white schematic labelled “Figure 8.10 – Definition of spacing for staples.” It shows a single row of staples embedded in a timber member, with all key dimensions and the grain direction annotated.  The main elements and annotations are as follows:

1. Timber boundaries  
   • Two horizontal parallel lines represent the top and bottom faces of a rectangular wood element. These lines run across the full width of the drawing.  

2. Grain‐direction arrow  
   • On the left side, between the two faces, there is a double-headed arrow pointing horizontally. This arrow is unlabelled but clearly indicates the fibre (grain) direction of the timber, which runs from left to right.

3. Staples  
   • Three identical staples are shown in a single row, parallel to the grain. Each staple is drawn with a short, thick black bar (the crown) just above the upper wood face, and two slender “legs” piercing downward into the timber.  
   • The legs are depicted as narrow lines terminating in small triangular tips, indicating the point-side penetration into the wood.  
   • The crowns of all three staples are rotated by the same angle Θ relative to the horizontal grain direction.

4. Angle Θ  
   • A curved leader from the crown of the central staple connects to the Greek letter Θ (Theta). This denotes the angle between the staple crown and the grain direction, as defined in the accompanying text (clause 8.3.2(5)).

5. Spacing dimensions  
   • Along the bottom of the timber, a horizontal dimension line with arrowheads at each end spans the distance between the centrelines of the first and the third staples. This distance is annotated “a₁.” It represents the minimum spacing between staples measured along the grain.  
   • On the right side of the drawing, two identical vertical dimension lines run from each staple leg tip to the nearest horizontal wood face. Both are annotated “a₂.” These indicate the minimum end-distance (edge distance) from a staple’s penetration point to the wood surface perpendicular to the grain.

6. Caption  
   • Below the schematic, the figure caption reads: “Figure 8.10 – Definition of spacing for staples,” reinforcing that the drawing specifically illustrates how to measure and maintain required clearances when arranging staples in a timber connection.

Overall, the diagram conveys three primary requirements for a row of staples parallel to the grain:
• The in-row spacing (centre-to-centre) must be at least a₁.  
• The distance from each penetration point to the wood’s top or bottom edge must be at least a₂.  
• Each staple crown must maintain an angle Θ relative to the grain, with this orientation affecting design load capacity as specified elsewhere in the standard.

content:
Below is a thorough, self-contained description of Table 8.3, which defines the minimum allowable spacings, edge distances and end distances for staple fasteners in timber connections. All dimensions are expressed as multiples of the staple-leg diameter d, and angles α refer to the orientation of the staple crown relative to the grain direction of the timber (see Figure 8.10 in the source).

1. General notation  
   • d: diameter of the staple legs, in mm (for rectangular cross-sections use d = √(b₁·b₂)).  
   • α: angle between the staple crown and the grain direction, measured in the plane of the timber face.  
   • θ: angle under the staple crown between the crown axis and the grain; used to distinguish two cases for parallel-to-grain spacing.  

2. Spacing and edge/end-distance parameters  
   – s₁: spacing between staples in a row parallel to the grain  
   – s₂: spacing between staples in a row perpendicular to the grain  
   – s₃,ₜ: distance from a loaded end of the timber member  
   – s₃,𝚌: distance from an unloaded end of the timber member  
   – s₄,ₜ: distance from a loaded edge (side) of the timber member  
   – s₄,𝚌: distance from an unloaded edge (side) of the timber member  

3. Table breakdown  

 Row  
  Angle range (α)  
  Minimum spacing or edge/end distance  

• s₁ (parallel to grain)  
  – for θ ≥ 30° (i.e. staple crown makes ≥ 30° with grain under the crown):  
    α can be anywhere from 0° to 360°.  
    s₁,min = (10 + 5·|cos α|)·d  
  – for θ < 30° (i.e. crown nearly aligned with grain):  
    same α-range 0°–360°, but increased base distance:  
    s₁,min = (15 + 5·|cos α|)·d  

  Interpretation: when staples sit almost parallel to grain beneath the crown (θ < 30°), spacing in the grain direction must be larger to reduce splitting risk. The cosine term modulates the spacing depending on the crown’s rotation: largest spacing when crown is parallel to grain (|cos α| = 1), smallest when at 90° (|cos α| = 0).

• s₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
  – α = 0° … 360°  
  – s₂,min = 15·d  

  Regardless of crown orientation, staples in the cross-grain direction need a constant spacing of 15 d to ensure adequate load distribution and avoid edge failures.

• s₃,ₜ (loaded end distance)  
  – α = –90° … +90° (staples whose crown points toward the loaded end)  
  – s₃,ₜ,min = (15 + 5·|cos α|)·d  

  Loaded ends impose higher tension or shear concentrations; hence a base of 15 d plus an orientation-dependent term.

• s₃,𝚌 (unloaded end distance)  
  – α = 90° … 270° (crowns pointing toward the “unloaded” or free end)  
  – s₃,𝚌,min = 15·d  

  Staples near an unloaded end still require a minimum embedment but no extra orientation penalty.

• s₄,ₜ (loaded edge distance)  
  – α = 0° … 180° (crowns pointing toward the loaded side edge)  
  – s₄,ₜ,min = (15 + 5·|sin α|)·d  

  Side edges loaded by out-of-plane forces need increased spacing; sin α models how crown orientation affects splitting risk across the edge.

• s₄,𝚌 (unloaded edge distance)  
  – α = 180° … 360° (crowns pointing toward the unloaded edge)  
  – s₄,𝚌,min = 10·d  

  A smaller constant distance suffices where the edge is not directly loaded.

4. How to apply these values in design  
  – Always measure α in the timber face plane, from the grain direction to the crown axis.  
  – Check θ (angle under the crown) only for s₁; for all other rows α fully captures orientation effects.  
  – Use the larger of the two values where more than one condition could apply (e.g. a staple near both an edge and end).  
  – These minimums work together with the capacity expressions for axial and lateral loads (see clauses 8.3.1.1–8.3.1.2 in the Eurocode context) to ensure both adequate strength and to avoid premature timber splitting or fastener yielding.

This structured summary can be indexed directly into a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store so that, given queries about staple placement rules, both the numeric formulas and the conceptual “when-to-use-which-row” logic are immediately retrievable.

The input “Table 8.4 – Minimum values of spacing and edge and end distances for bolts” defines, for a single bolted connection in timber or LVL, the minimum centre-to-centre spacing or edge/end distance required as a function of the bolt diameter d and the angle α between the line of action of the applied load and the wood grain.  All distances in the table are expressed as multiples of the bolt diameter d (unless an absolute millimetre value is given).  The table is laid out in three columns:

 1.  Spacing and end/edge distance  
 2.  Angle α (degrees): the orientation of the load direction relative to the grain (0° = parallel to grain, 90° = perpendicular to grain)  
 3.  Minimum spacing or distance (as a function of d and, in some cases, α)  

The individual rows are:

•  a₁ (parallel to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum spacing: (4 + |cos α|) · d  
     *This means that when the load is exactly parallel (α = 0° or 180°), cos α = ±1, |cos α| = 1 → a₁ = 5 d.  When the load is perpendicular (α = 90° or 270°), |cos α| = 0 → a₁ = 4 d.  In intermediate directions the spacing varies smoothly between these extremes.*  

•  a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum spacing: 4 d (constant, independent of α)  

•  a₃,t (loaded end distance)  
   – Angle range: –90° ≤ α ≤ 90°  
   – Minimum end distance: max(7 d ; 80 mm)  
     *Use whichever is the larger value: seven times the bolt diameter or 80 mm.*  

•  a₃,c (unloaded end distance)  
   – Three sub-ranges of α:  
     1.  90° ≤ α < 150° → minimum = max([1 + 6 sin α]·d ; 4 d)  
     2.  150° ≤ α < 210° → minimum = 4 d  
     3.  210° ≤ α ≤ 270° → minimum = max([1 + 6 sin α]·d ; 4 d)  
     *Here sin α is taken in radians, so for 90° < α < 150° the required distance increases from 7 d at  α=90° down to 4 d at α=150°, then remains constant at 4 d until 210°, and then mirrors the first segment for 210°<α<270°.*  

•  a₄,t (loaded edge distance)  
   – Angle range: 0° ≤ α ≤ 180°  
   – Minimum edge distance: max([2 + 2 sin α]·d ; 3 d)  
     *At α=0° or 180°, sin α=0 → requirement is max(2 d;3 d)=3 d.  At α=90°, sin α=1 → requirement is max(4 d;3 d)=4 d.*  

•  a₄,c (unloaded edge distance)  
   – Angle range: 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
   – Minimum edge distance: 3 d (constant)  

Notes and cross-references:  
- All “max(…, …)” expressions mean the larger of the two bracketed distances is to be used.  
- α is measured from the grain direction: 0° when the load is exactly parallel to the grain, increasing through 90° when perpendicular, up to 360°.  
- Figure 8.7 (not shown) illustrates the geometric definitions of a₁ through a₄ with respect to the bolt and the timber member outline.  
- This spacing table complements the characteristic embedment strengths and yield-moment formulae for bolts given elsewhere (see clauses 8.1.2 and 10.4.3).

The table excerpted as “Table 8.5 – Minimum spacings and edge and end distances for dowels” provides, for each defined dowel-to-dowel or dowel-to-edge configuration,  
1) a symbol (a₁, a₂, a₃, etc.) and its meaning,  
2) the range of load-angle α (in degrees) over which that rule applies, and  
3) the formula or fixed value giving the required minimum centre-to-centre spacing or the minimum distance to an unloaded edge/end.  

This table must be interpreted in conjunction with:  
• The general rules of Section 8.5.1 (excluding only 8.5.1.1(3)),  
• A dowel diameter d strictly between 6 mm and 30 mm,  
• The symbol definitions shown in Figure 8.7, and  
• The hole-tolerance requirements of Section 10.4.4.  

1) Column headings  
   – “Spacing and edge/end distances (see Figure 8.7)” lists each spacing variable and whether it refers to parallel/perpendicular spacing or to distance from a loaded or unloaded edge or end.  
   – “Angle” gives the angular range 0° to 360°, or sub-ranges thereof, over which the particular spacing rule applies.  
   – “Minimum spacing or edge/end distance” gives either a formula in terms of the dowel diameter d and the loading angle α, or a fixed multiple of d (and occasionally an absolute cap in mm).  

2) Row-by-row description  

 a₁ (parallel to grain)  
   • Applies for any load angle α from 0° to 360°.  
   • Minimum centre-to-centre spacing = (3 + 2 |cos α|) d  
     – When the dowel axis is aligned parallel to the grain (α=0° or 180°), |cos α|=1 so the spacing is 5 d.  
     – When α=90° or 270°, |cos α|=0 so spacing is 3 d.  

 a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
   • Applies for any α from 0° to 360°.  
   • Spacing is constant at 3 d, irrespective of angle.  

 a₃,ₜ (loaded end)  
   • For angles –90° ≤ α ≤ 90°, this governs the minimum distance from the loaded end face.  
   • Minimum distance = max(7 d; 80 mm).  
     – Ensures either a multiple of the dowel diameter or an absolute minimum of 80 mm, whichever is greater.  

 a₃,𝑐 (unloaded end)  
   • Splits into three sub-ranges of α:  
     90° ≤ α < 150°,  
     150° ≤ α ≤ 210°,  
     210° ≤ α ≤ 270°.  
   • For the first and third sub-ranges:  
     minimum distance = max(a₃,ₜ · |sin α| · d; 3 d).  
   • For 150° ≤ α ≤ 210°:  
     distance is a constant 3 d.  
   • This ensures that when the loading is principally toward the “unloaded” end, spacing relaxes to 3 d, but when the loading vector has a substantial axial component, the distance scales with |sin α|.  

 a₄,ₜ (loaded edge)  
   • For angles 0° ≤ α ≤ 180°, this is the minimum side-edge distance at the loaded edge.  
   • Spacing = max([2 + 2 sin α] d; 3 d).  
     – When α is small, sin α is small, so the rule defaults to 3 d. As α approaches 90°, sin α→1 and the required distance becomes up to 4 d.  

 a₄,𝑐 (unloaded edge)  
   • Applies for 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°, i.e. when the load is directed toward the opposite (“unloaded”) edge.  
   • Minimum distance is fixed at 3 d.  

3) How to use these rules in practice  
   1. Identify the loading direction α with respect to the dowel’s principal axes (grain direction and end faces).  
   2. For each neighbouring dowel or plate edge/face, determine whether the neighbour is parallel/perpendicular to grain, an end or an edge, and whether it is “loaded” or “unloaded” by the applied force.  
   3. Consult the corresponding row of Table 8.5 using the appropriate angle range.  
   4. Compute the formula (or take the fixed multiple) to find the minimum allowable spacing or edge distance in terms of dowel diameter d.  
   5. Ensure no 8.5.1 rule violations occur elsewhere, and that the dowel holes meet the tolerances of Section 10.4.4.  

By following this structured procedure, one ensures that dowels are sufficiently spaced apart and sufficiently far from edges and ends, accounting for directional loads and maintaining the integrity and strength of the timber connection.

(1) The rules given in 8.5.1 except 8.5.1.1(3) apply.
 (2) The dowel diameter should be greater than 6 mm and less than 30 mm.
 (3) Minimum spacing and edge and end distances are given in Table 8.5, with symbols illustrated in Figure 8.7.
 (4) Requirements for dowel hole tolerances are given in 10.4.4.

(1)P Connections made with punched metal plate fasteners shall comprise punched metal plate fasteners of the same type, size and orientation, placed on each side of the timber members.
 (2) The following rules apply only to punched metal plate fasteners with two orthogonal directions.

The figure shows a punched metal plate connector joining two timber members and subject to an externally applied force (F Ed) and bending moment (M Ed).  A global right-hand Cartesian coordinate system (x, y) is drawn with the x-axis horizontal and y-axis vertical.  The connector plate spans the interface between two pieces of timber, here schematically sketched as “member 1” above the plate and “member 2” below.  The plate itself is represented by a filled rectangle patterned with small slots (the nail or screw holes), and its “effective area” (the region over which load is transferred into the wood) is outlined by a dashed-dot border (key label 1).  

Key features and annotations:
• Grain directions (key label 2) in the two wood members are shown by arrows angled relative to the plate.  In the upper member the grain runs roughly perpendicular to the plate, in the lower member it is inclined at an angle β below the dashed-line reference axis.  
• The resultant design load F Ed is applied at the mid-span of the connector and oriented at an angle α above the horizontal x-axis.  
• The bending moment M Ed, acting about the z-axis (out of the plane), is indicated by a curved arrow pointing counter-clockwise.  This moment induces additional tensile and compressive forces at the opposing edges of the effective area.  
• These forces due to the moment are denoted F M,Ed and are drawn at the top and bottom corners of the plate’s effective area, each directed toward the plate at an oblique angle.  The angle γ between F M,Ed and the effective-area border is also shown.  
• A dimension ℓ is marked along the line of action of F Ed, measured from the plate’s mid-thickness to the centre of rotation corresponding to M Ed.  

Together, F Ed and M Ed resolve into tension, compression and shear components on the connector plate.  The plate’s characteristic capacities (anchorage per unit area and tension, compression and shear per unit width for two principal orientations α = 0°/90° and β = 0°/90°) are determined by tests in accordance with EN 1075 and evaluated under EN 14545.  In design, these capacities are combined using the modification factor k mod = 1.0 to calculate the required plate thickness, embedment length and fastener arrangement so that neither the plate nor the surrounding timber fails under the combined loading.

Overall, the image provides both the governing equation for the shear capacity of ring-type connectors and the geometric requirements—connector diameter, embedment depth, and timber thicknesses—necessary to comply with EN standard rules for split-ring/shear-plate connections in timber.

sections: 8.9  Split ring and shear plate connectors

content:
Below is a structured, self-contained description of the entries in Table 8.7 (“Minimum spacings and edge and end distances for ring and shear plate connectors”) together with the relevant context from EN 912 and EN 14545. Wherever a spacing is expressed in terms of the connector diameter dc, α denotes the angle between the connector axis and the grain direction of the timber member.

1. Scope and basic assumption  
   • Applies to ring connectors of type A or shear-plate connectors of type B (EN 912/EN 14545) with dc ≤ 200 mm.  
   • All distances are characteristic minimum values to prevent splitting or excessive stress concentrations.

2. Column headings in Table 8.7  
   – “Spacing and edge/end distances”: the variable symbol and a short descriptor (see schematic in Figure 8.7).  
   – “Angle to grain”: the range of α (in degrees) over which the formula applies.  
   – “Minimum spacings and edge/end distances”: the formula or constant multiplied by dc.

3. Rows (variables a₁ to a₄,c)  

   a) a₁ (parallel to grain)  
     • α from 0° to 360°  
     • a₁ = (1.2 + 0.8 · |cos α|) · dc  

   b) a₂ (perpendicular to grain)  
     • α from 0° to 360°  
     • a₂ = 1.2 · dc  

   c) a₃,t (loaded end distance)  
     • α from –90° to +90°  
     • a₃,t = 1.5 · dc  

   d) a₃,c (unloaded end distance)  
     • 90° ≤ α < 150°: a₃,c = (0.4 + 1.6 · |sin α|) · dc  
     • 150° ≤ α < 210°: a₃,c = 1.2 · dc  
     • 210° ≤ α < 270°: a₃,c = (0.4 + 1.6 · |sin α|) · dc  

   e) a₄,t (loaded edge distance)  
     • 0° ≤ α ≤ 180°  
     • a₄,t = (0.6 + 0.2 · |sin α|) · dc  

   f) a₄,c (unloaded edge distance)  
     • 180° ≤ α ≤ 360°  
     • a₄,c = 0.6 · dc  

4. Staggered connectors (clause 10, eq. 8.69)  
   • When connectors are staggered in plan (see Figure 8.13), the minimum spacings parallel (effective a₁') and perpendicular (a₂') to grain may be reduced via factors kₐ₁ and kₐ₂ subject to  
     (kₐ₁·a₁)² + (kₐ₂·a₂)² ≥ 1.  
   • kₐ₁ and kₐ₂ range between 0 and 1, reducing the clearances provided the combined condition is met.

5. Further reduction of parallel spacing (clause 11, eq. 8.70)  
   • The spacing a₁ parallel to grain may be multiplied by a reduction factor kₛ,red (0.5 ≤ kₛ,red ≤ 1.0).  
   • If spacing is reduced in this way, the characteristic load-carrying capacity FBv,0,RkB (per connector, per shear plane) shall be multiplied by  
     R,red = 0.8 + 0.2·kₛ,red.  

6. Effective number of connectors (clause 12)  
   • For a row of n connectors aligned parallel to grain, an “effective number” nₑff is used to calculate the total load-carrying capacity in that direction.  
   • The reduction accounts for interaction effects when connector spacing is smaller than recommended values.

7. Parallel‐orientation criterion (clause 13)  
   • A connector is treated as “parallel to grain” if its unloaded-side spacing a₄,c (perp.) is less than 0.5·a₁ (parallel). In that case, design formulas for a₁ govern its behavior.

––––  
This description translates Table 8.7 into a narrative form, clarifies the angle-dependent formulas for minimum distances, and incorporates the reduction factors and effective-connector-number concept from the adjoining clauses of EN 912/EN 14545.
