The figure shows a schematic cross-section through a wood member (two horizontal lines at top and bottom) in which two circular connectors have been placed in a staggered arrangement. It is labelled “Figure 8.13 – Reduced distances for connectors” and is intended to illustrate how the minimum spacing parallel and perpendicular to the grain may be reduced by factors k­a1 and k­a2.  

Overall layout:  
• The wood element is represented by two straight, horizontal parallel lines (top and bottom). These define the grain direction, which runs horizontally, and the thickness of the member between them.  
• Two circles, of equal diameter, represent the ring or shear‐plate connectors inserted through the member. One circle is positioned toward the left side, closer to the bottom line; the other is positioned more to the right and nearer the mid-height of the section.  
• Each circle has a pair of dashed centerlines: a vertical centerline trough its center, and a horizontal centerline. These help to measure offsets in the two orthogonal directions.  

Dimensioning arrows and labels:  
1. Horizontal spacing:  
   - Two vertical, thin dashed reference lines are drawn through the vertical centerlines of each circle.  
   - Between these two reference lines, a double-headed horizontal arrow is shown. Above that arrow is the composite label “k­a1 a1.” This indicates that the original minimum spacing parallel to the grain (a1) has been multiplied by the reduction factor k­a1.  
2. Vertical spacing:  
   - A horizontal, thin dashed reference line is drawn through the center of the right‐hand circle. From this line, a double-headed vertical arrow drops down to the center of the left‐hand circle. Adjacent to this arrow is the label “k­a2 a2,” indicating that the original spacing perpendicular to the grain (a2) is reduced by factor k­a2.  

Interpretation in context:  
According to the EN timber‐fastener standards cited in the accompanying text (EN 912, EN 14545), when connectors of type A or type B with diameter ≤200 mm are installed in a staggered pattern, their spacing parallel and perpendicular to the grain may be reduced. The reduction factors k­a1 (parallel) and k­a2 (perpendicular) must satisfy the interaction rule:  
   (k­a1 / a1)² + (k­a2 / a2)² ≥ 1     (equation 8.69)  
Thus the figure graphically shows the two reduced spacings k­a1 a1 and k­a2 a2 and their geometric relationship in a staggered connector layout.  

Additional notes drawn from the text:  
– k­a1 and k­a2 are both between 0 and 1 (with different bounds depending on the factor).  
– Further reductions in a1 (parallel spacing) by a k­s,red factor between 0.5 and 1.0 are possible, provided the connector capacity is amplified by R,red = 0.8 + 0.2·k­s,red (equation 8.70).  
– In a straight row of connectors parallel to the grain, the effective number of connectors is used to calculate capacity.  
– This figure helps the designer verify that even with reduced spacing, the connectors will not interact too closely and the combined load‐carrying capacity remains adequate.

A key at the bottom of the figure denotes label “1” as compression and label “2” as tension.

1. Left-hand view (cross section about neutral axis)  
   • Overall shape: a classic I-section in cross section, but with very narrow (thin) web plates connecting two substantially wider flanges.  
   • Flanges:  
     – Two rectangular flange blocks, one at the top and one at the bottom. Each block has its long axis horizontal (width direction).  
     – Each flange block carries the label “1” on the side facing the viewer. According to the key, this indicates that these are the regions in compression under the assumed bending. (Top flange in compression, bottom flange likewise labeled “1,” though the key suggests bottom might be in tension depending on loading.)  
   • Web:  
     – A narrow vertical plate (the “thin web”) connects the two flanges. Its width is much smaller than the flange width.  
     – The narrow web region is centered on the same vertical mid-plane as the flanges.  
   • Dimensioning (bottom of view):  
     – A pair of horizontal dimension arrows span the total width of the section and are labeled “b.”  
     – Immediately adjacent to the web, a shorter dimension arrow indicates the web thickness (or width) labeled “b_w.”  

2. Center view (side-elevation of the same I-section)  
   • Outline: shows a rectangular perimeter corresponding to the two flanges plus the web in between, viewed from the side (depth into the page is constant).  
   • Internal web stiffeners: two or three thin vertical lines inside the outline represent the web stiffeners or panel seams, equally spaced in the web height. Each is again labeled “1,” indicating compression zones under design loading (consistent with flanges in the cross section).  
   • Height subdivisions:  
     – Top flange thickness (vertical height of top block) is shown by a vertical dimension arrow annotated “h_f,c.” The subscript “c” denotes the compressive flange thickness.  
     – The clear web height is shown by a pair of arrows pointing to the gap between flanges and labeled “h_w.”  
     – Bottom flange thickness is by another arrow pair labeled “h_f,t,” where “t” denotes the tensile flange.  
   • Width dimensions (along bottom):  
     – The same two arrows from the cross section appear, showing total width “b” and web width “b_w.”  

3. Right-hand view (axial‐stress distribution diagram)  
   • The drawing is a triangular (or trapezoidal) stress profile plotted over the beam depth. The vertical axis represents depth; the horizontal axis represents stress magnitude.  
   • Peak compressive stress at the top fiber is labeled σ_f,c,max,d (extreme-fiber design compressive stress). A short horizontal line at the apex indicates its magnitude.  
   • Peak tensile stress at the bottom fiber is labeled σ_f,t,max,d (extreme-fiber design tensile stress). A corresponding horizontal line at the bottom shows that maximum tensile stress.  
   • A linear line connecting these two outer points represents the assumed linear variation of strain (and hence stress) across the section depth. The neutral axis, midway between top and bottom, crosses the zero‐stress plane.  
   • Additionally, two smaller rectangular blocks (one in the upper half and one in the lower half) depict the mean flange stresses σ_f,c,d (upper block) and σ_f,t,d (lower block). These are the average compressive and tensile stresses over the flange depths.  
   • The right-hand margin indicates half-depth dimensions (“h_f,c/2” above neutral axis, “h_f,t/2” below) to show how mean stresses relate to flange thickness.  

4. Caption and Key  
   • Below all three views, the label reads “Figure 9.1 – Thin-webbed beams.”  
   • At the very bottom a short key states:  
     – (1) compression  
     – (2) tension  

Taken together, this figure illustrates (a) the geometry of a thin-web I-beam made from wood-based panels, (b) the dimensional parameters that enter into design verifications (flange widths, web width, flange depths, web depth), and (c) the linear stress distribution under bending—emphasizing both extreme-fiber and mean stresses in the flanges.

The illustration is labelled “Figure 9.2 – Thin-flanged beam” and shows both the top and bottom flange layouts together with the location of the webs that form an I-shaped cross-section.  In what follows the beam is assumed to have wood-based flanges and wood-based panel webs, with a linear strain profile over the overall depth.  

General layout  
• Two continuous horizontal members (flanges) run along the length of the beam, one at the top and one at the bottom.  
• Between these flanges are three identical vertical web panels, equally spaced, carrying shear and axial forces.  
• Each web is indexed “1,” indicating the location of the sectional check (section 1-1) referred to in the design rules.  

Top flange detail  
• The total effective flange width is denoted b_ef.  
• On the compression-face (top flange under positive bending), the effective width is written as b_c,ef.  This width is subdivided by the webs into three segments, each of width b_c,ef/2 on either side of each web and between webs.  Arrows marking b_c,ef/2 are shown on both sides of each web location.  
• Over the span of two panel-spaces (that is, across two webs and the intermediate flange panel), the dimension b_ef is called out.  It encompasses the three flange segments (each b_c,ef/2 plus b_c,ef/2) plus the two web-separations in between.  

Bottom flange detail  
• Analogous notation appears directly below the web stack for the tension face of the beam (bottom flange).  Here the effective flange width is b_t,ef and its half-widths b_t,ef/2 are again shown to either side of each web.  
• The overall width of the bottom flange for two panel-spaces is likewise marked b_ef (same as top).  

Web and panel spacing  
• At the very bottom, a longitudinal dimension line shows the sum of flange panel widths and web widths for two consecutive bays.  The flange panel width is labelled b_f; the web panel width is b_w.  Thus one bay is b_f + b_w, and two bays b_f + b_w + b_f.  
• Vertical lines (slightly thicker) denote the webs; lighter horizontal shading represents flange panels.  

Annotations and references  
• The three identical web panels are each marked with the numeral “1,” tying them to the “section 1-1” checks in clause 9.1.1 for axial stresses in webs of wood-based panels.  
• Dimension arrows all point outward from the member edges or from the web-flange interfaces, making clear the effective widths to be used in the stress verifications.  
• The figure underpins the expressions (9.6) to (9.7) for axial stresses in wood-based webs, in the same way that the earlier flange stress expressions (9.1) to (9.4) apply to the flanges.  

Overall, Figure 9.2 provides a clear, to-scale schematic for:

2. Identifying the individual webs (section 1-1) whose axial stresses must be checked against the design criteria for wood-based panel webs.

The figure presents a plan view of a rectangular diaphragm loaded by a uniformly distributed lateral pressure and supported at its ends.  Key graphic elements and annotations are described below:

1. Overall Geometry  
   - A rectangle represents the diaphragm panel assembly, with its long horizontal side labeled “ℓ” (span) and the vertical dimension labeled “b” (width).  
   - At the top of the rectangle, a row of closely spaced, downward‐pointing arrows indicates the uniformly distributed load acting across the full width of the diaphragm.

2. Support Reactions  
   - At each end of the span (left and right), a single large upward arrow denotes the reaction at the edge beams or supporting elements.  

3. Nail or Fastener Lines (Label “(1)”)  
   - Immediately inside the top boundary of the rectangle, a dashed line runs across the full length. This dashed line, tagged “(1),” represents the line of fasteners or connections along the panel edges where shear is transferred into the supporting beams.

4. Edge Beams or Continuous Panel Edges (Label “(2)”)  
   - At both the left and right ends of the diaphragm, solid‐filled rectangular strips are shown running full width (from top to bottom). These are annotated “(2)” and identify edge beam locations or continuous panel assemblies that anchor the diaphragm into the supporting structure.

5. Staggered Panel Arrangement (Label “(3)”)  
   - In the central portion of the diaphragm, two distinct panel layouts are illustrated side by side:  
     • On the left half, individual sheet panels are staggered so that vertical joints do not line up from row to row. This “brick‐bond” pattern is pointed to by arrow “(3).”  
     • On the right half, panels are shown in uniform vertical alignment (continuous joints), emphasizing the contrast with the staggered layout.

6. Notation of Design Guidance  
   - Beneath the graphic, the caption reads “Figure 9.4 – Diaphragm loading and staggered panel arrangements.” This ties back to the accompanying text, which specifies conditions under which the simplified analysis applies (span-to-width ratio, fastener failure mode, plate fixing details), the requirement to design edge beams for maximum bending moment, the assumption of uniformly distributed shear, and the allowance for increased nail spacing along staggered edges.

Overall, the diagram conveys how a wood‐ or sheathed‐panel diaphragm should be loaded, supported, and detailed—particularly highlighting the fastener line, edge beam condition, and the effect of staggered versus continuous panel joints on load transfer.

 — the span @ lies between 24 and 6b, where b is the diaphragm width;

(1)P Wall diaphragms shall be designed to resist both horizontal and vertical actions imposed upon them.
 (2)P The wall shall be adequately restrained to avoid overturning and sliding.
 (3)P Wall diaphragms deemed to provide resistance to racking shall be stiffened in-plane by board materials, diagonal bracing or moment connections.
 (4)P The racking resistance of a wall shall be determined either by test according to EN 594 or by calculations, employing appropriate analytical methods or design models.
 (5)P The design of wall diaphragms shall take account of both the material construction and geometric make-up of the wall under consideration.
 (6)P The response of wall diaphragms to actions shall be assessed to ensure the construction remains within appropriate serviceability limits.
 (7) For wall diaphragms two alternative simplified methods of calculation are given in 9.2.4.2 and 9.2.4.3.
 NOTE: The recommended procedure is method A given in 9.2.4.2. National choice may be given in the National annex.

The illustration is divided into two schematic sub-figures, “a)” on the left and “b)” on the right, and is captioned “Figure 9.5 – Forces acting on: a) wall panel; b) framing; c) sheet.”  Together they show how design racking and vertical forces are applied to a timber-framed wall panel and how those forces are taken by the framing and by the sheathing.

1. Sub-figure a) Wall Panel  
   • Geometry: A single rectangular wall panel of height h (vertical dimension, not explicitly annotated here) and width bᵢ (horizontal dimension), indicated by a double-headed arrow at the top spanning the full panel width, labelled “bᵢ.”  
   • Studs: Two vertical studs are sketched inside the panel as narrow vertical rectangles, shown with dashed lines to indicate their hidden or interior position behind the sheathing.  
   • Applied Forces:  
     – Fᵢ,ᵥ,Ed: A pair of horizontal arrows at top (pushing in from the right) and at mid-height on the left (pushing in from the left) indicate the lateral (racking) design force acting on the panel. Both arrows are labelled “Fᵢ,ᵥ,Ed.”  
     – Fᵢ,c,Ed: At the bottom left corner an arrow pointing downward (into the panel) is labelled “Fᵢ,c,Ed,” representing the compressive vertical design force at that corner.  
     – Fᵢ,t,Ed: At the bottom right corner an arrow pointing upward (tension) is labelled “Fᵢ,t,Ed,” representing the tensile vertical design force.  
   • Interpretation: This view abstracts the wall panel as a free-body: lateral load at the top drives racking, while vertical reactions (compression and tension) are taken at the panel ends.

2. Sub-figure b) Framing and Sheathing Force Paths  
   • Outline: A taller rectangle represents the timber frame seen face-on; a central stud splits it into two bays.  
   • Framing members: The outer perimeter and the central stud are drawn as solid thick lines, showing the stud positions and boundary plates.  
   • Sheathing (sheet): A lighter, maybe dashed or ghosted overlay indicates the position of the sheet material fixed to one side of the frame.  
   • Force‐flow arrows: A continuous chain of small arrowheads runs around the inside perimeter of the frame and then, in dashed form, around the perimeter of the sheet—demonstrating how lateral shear from the sheet is transferred through the fasteners into the framing and around to the opposite side.  
   • Corner detail: In the upper left corner a small square indicates the corner of the framing, where force changes direction. Arrowheads turn the corner, showing that the panel’s racking load is taken by the frame at its edges and carried around the boundary.  

Overall the figure shows:  
– How the design racking resistance Fᵢ,ᵥ,Rd is evaluated for a single panel of width bᵢ, stiffness and spacing of fasteners s, and the resulting vertical forces at panel ends.  
– How the sheet transfers shear into the frame via perimeter fasteners, with the load path running continuously around the edges (and stud supports where present).  
– The necessity of tension and compression anchorage at the panel base (see Fᵢ,c,Ed and Fᵢ,t,Ed) so that uplift or overturning due to racking is resisted.  

By combining the free‐body panel loads in a) with the force‐flow diagram in b), the standard’s simplified method of analysis (Clauses 9.2.4.2(3–5)) can be applied to calculate the design racking capacity of wall diaphragms, ensuring that fastener spacing, panel width, and anchorage are all accounted for.

sections: 9.2.4.2  Simplified analysis of wall diaphragms – Method A

The image is a schematic elevation view (Figure 9.6) of a linear assembly of timber wall panels under a horizontal racking load.  From left to right the panels are laid out in the sequence: normal-width panel (1), normal-width panel (1), window-opening panel (2), normal-width panel (1), normal-width panel (1), smaller-width panel (3), and a final normal-width panel (1).  Two large horizontal arrows at each end of the assembly indicate the design racking force (labelled Fv,Ed) applied to the panel line: one arrow pushing from the left, the other reacting on the right.  

Each panel is drawn with its vertical timber studs shown as solid lines; the sheathing sheets are implied by the overall panel outline, with light dashed vertical lines marking the constant fastener spacing along each edge.  In most panels diagonal lines sloping upwards from left to right denote the bracing action of the sheathing resisting shear.  In the window panel (2), two rectangular cut‐outs represent the window openings, flanked above and below by shorter sections of sheathed wall.  The smaller-width panel (3) is narrower than the normal panels and is also braced.  

Below the drawing a dimension line spanning one normal panel is labelled bi, the gross panel width.  Between two adjacent studs of opposite panels a smaller dimension bnet (the clear stud‐to‐stud spacing) is shown.  Underneath the entire assembly runs a key identifying the panel types:  
• (1) Wall panel (normal width)  
• (2) Wall panel with window opening  
• (3) Wall panel (smaller width)  

At each interface between panels—and at the ends—short vertical arrows indicate possible paths for the lateral shear forces Fi,c,Ed or Fi,t,Ed to transmit either into the adjacent panel or into the supporting construction above or below.  The figure thus illustrates how, in a multi‐panel timber wall, some panels (type 1) contribute their full racking capacity, panels containing openings (type 2) do not contribute to shear resistance, and narrower panels (type 3) may contribute a reduced amount.  

The constant fastener spacing (shown by the dashed lines) and the requirement that no panel be narrower than h/4 are implicit in the layout.  The notation bnet reminds the designer to check the clear span for sheet shear buckling (per clause 9.2.4.2(11)), while the arrows at the panel ends signal the need for tie-down or anchoring against uplift (clause 9.2.4.2(1)).  Overall, the drawing encapsulates the simplified method for assembling and analysing a series of wall panels—normal, windowed, and narrow—subject to lateral loading, consistent with the equations and factors set out in the preceding subclauses.

The image is a schematic line drawing (Figure 9.7) illustrating a typical timber‐framed wall assembly composed of five separate panels, which together form three distinct wall segments. Horizontally, the full assembly (9) stretches from left to right and is subdivided into Wall 1 (6), Wall 2 (7) and Wall 3 (8). Within those walls, individual panels are numbered sequentially: Wall 1 contains Wall panel 1 (1) and Wall panel 2 (2); Wall 2 contains Wall panel 3 (3) and Wall panel 4 (4); Wall 3 comprises Wall panel 5 (5).  

Each wall panel is constructed from timber studs and top/bottom plates, onto which sheets of wood-based panel products (10) are fastened. The diagonal lines on each panel represent these sheathing sheets, and each sheet is shown attached around its perimeter and within its field by regularly spaced fasteners, consistent with the requirement that interior fasteners be no farther apart than twice the perimeter spacing. Across the top of the panels runs a continuous head binder (11), depicted as a solid horizontal member that ties the top edges of adjacent panels, providing the specified minimum vertical connection strength of 2.5 kN/m at the joints.

Openings in the panels are clearly marked: Wall panel 3 features a rectangular window opening (12), framed by additional short studs, header and sill members; Wall panel 4 includes a door opening (13), likewise framed by a header and jack studs. In accordance with the design rules, each side of these openings is treated as an independent “separate panel” for racking strength calculations and fastening layout. The dimension arrows at the bottom of the drawing indicate the widths of panels (1) through (5), the aggregate lengths of Walls 1, 2 and 3, and the total length of the wall assembly.

Key aspects highlighted by the drawing and reinforced by the accompanying text are:
- Panel sizing and layout: Each panel’s width is at least one quarter of its height, ensuring adequate in-plane (racking) capacity.
- Fastening pattern: Nails or screws are equally spaced around each sheathing sheet’s perimeter, with internal fasteners spaced at no more than twice the perimeter interval.
- Panel joining: The head binder (11) straddles panel joints to develop the required vertical and lateral load path, resisting overturning and sliding through a combination of anchorage details and permanent loading.
- Treatment of openings: Window (12) and door (13) openings subdivide panels into smaller effective panels for strength verification.
- Multi-panel wall behavior: When combined, panels form longer walls that must be anchored or otherwise loaded to resist design force combinations, tying into adjacent structure or relying on permanent actions.

Overall, the figure serves as a clear example of how individual sheets and frames are arranged, fastened and connected to produce a robust, racking-resistant wall assembly in timber construction.

sections: 9.2.4.3  Simplified analysis of wall diaphragms – Method B
9.2.4.3.1  Construction of walls and panels to meet the requirements of the simplified  analysis

content:
(1) A wall assembly (see Figure 9.7) is comprised of one or more walls with each wall formed from one or more panels, the panels being made from sheets of wood-based panel products, such as those described in 3.5, fastened to a timber frame.
 (2) For a panel to contribute to the in-plane (racking) strength of a wall the width of the panel should be at least the panel height divided by 4. The fastening of the sheets to the timber frame should be by either nails or screws and the fasteners should be equally spaced around the perimeter of the sheet. Fasteners within the perimeter of a sheet should be spaced at not more than twice the perimeter fastener spacing.
 (3) Where an opening is formed in a panel, the lengths of panel on each side of the opening should be considered as separate panels.
 (4) Where panels are combined to form a wall:
 − the tops of individual panels should be linked by a member or construction across the panel joints;
 −
 the required vertical connection strength between two panels should be evaluated but should have a design strength of at least 2,5 kN/m;
 − the panels when joined together to form a wall should be able to resist overturning and sliding forces by either anchorage to the supporting structure or the permanent actions applied to the wall or a combination of both effects.

content: (1)P The provisions given in this section are prerequisite requirements for the design rules given in this standard to apply.

(1) The deviation from straightness measured midway between the supports should, for columns and beams where lateral instability can occur, or members in frames, be limited to 1/500 times the length of glued laminated timber or LVL members and to 1/300 times the length of solid timber. The limitations on bow in most strength grading rules are inadequate for the selection of material for these members and particular attention should therefore be paid to their straightness.
 (2) Timber and wood-based components and structural elements should not be unnecessarily exposed to climatic conditions more severe than those expected in the finished structure.
 (3) Before being used in construction, timber should be dried as near as practicable to the moisture content appropriate to its climatic condition in the completed structure. If the effects of any shrinkage are not considered important, or if parts that are unacceptably damaged are replaced, higher moisture contents may be accepted during erection provided that it is ensured that the timber can dry to the desired moisture content.

(1) Where bond strength is a requirement for ultimate limit state design, the manufacture of glued joints should be subject to quality control, to ensure that the reliability and quality of the joint is in accordance with the technical specification.
 (2) The adhesive manufacturer’s recommendations with respect to mixing, environmental conditions for application and curing, moisture content of members and all factors relevant to the proper use of the adhesive should be followed.
 (3) For adhesives which require a conditioning period after initial set, before attaining full strength, the application of load to the joint should be restricted for the necessary time.
(1)P Wane, splits, knots or other defects shall be limited in the region of the connection such that the load-carrying capacity of the connection is not reduced.

(1) Unless otherwise specified, nails should be driven in at right angles to the grain and to such depth that the surfaces of the nail heads are flush with the timber surface.
 (2) Unless otherwise specified, slant nailing should be carried out in accordance with Figure 8.8(b).
 (3) The diameter of pre-drilled holes should not exceed 0,8d, where d is the nail diameter.

The input is an excerpt from “Table 10.1 – Requirements for diameters of bolts used with timber connectors,” which defines minimum and maximum bolt‐diameters (d) for various connector categories (EN 912), based on the connector’s own diameter (dc) or the diameter of its centre hole (d₁).  The table is best understood in light of four explanatory notes:

 1.  Hole sizing (footnote 1):  
    – In timber, any bolt hole must exceed the bolt’s actual diameter by no more than 1 mm.  
    – In steel plates, the hole may exceed the bolt diameter by up to 2 mm or 0.1·d, whichever is greater.  

 2.  Washers (footnote 2):  
    Under both bolt heads and nuts, use washers whose diameter or side‐length is at least 3·d and whose thickness is at least 0.3·d, ensuring full bearing contact.

 3.  Tightening (footnote 3):  
    Bolts and lag screws must be snug so timber members bear tightly. After the timber reaches equilibrium moisture content, retighten as needed to preserve load capacity and structural stiffness.

 4.  Symbols (footnote 4):  
    – dc = connector outer diameter, in millimetres.  
    – d  = bolt diameter, in millimetres.  
    – d₁ = diameter of the connector’s centre hole, in millimetres.

Structure of Table 10.1:

 Columns:
 •  “Type of connector EN 912” lists connector classes (“A1 – A6,” or specific subsets “A1, A4, A6,” and “B”).  
 •  “dc (mm)” gives the size range or criterion applying to the connector’s body.  
 •  “d minimum (mm)” prescribes the smallest allowable bolt diameter.  
 •  “d maximum (mm)” prescribes the largest allowable bolt diameter.

 Rows:
 1.  A1 – A6 with dc ≤ 130 mm  
     – dmin = 12 mm  
     – dmax = 24 mm  

 2.  A1, A4, A6 with dc > 130 mm  
     – dmin = 0.1·dc (i.e. ten per cent of the connector’s diameter)  
     – dmax = 24 mm  

 3.  B (all dc)  
     – dmin = d₁ – 1 mm (one millimetre less than the centre‐hole diameter)  
     – dmax = d₁ (equal to the centre‐hole diameter)

Key points for RAG indexing:
 •  Connector categories are distinguished by EN 912 designations (A1–A6, A1/A4/A6, B).  
 •  The minimum bolt size for smaller connectors (dc ≤ 130 mm) is a fixed 12 mm, while larger A-series connectors scale the minimum by 0.1·dc.  
 •  All A-series connectors cap bolt diameter at 24 mm.  
 •  Category B uses the connector’s own hole size (d₁) to set bolt limits: from d₁ – 1 up to d₁.  
 •  Ensure hole drilling and washer use conform to the general rules in notes 1–3 to maintain correct fit and structural performance.

The drawing, titled “10.1 – Example of connection of panels not supported by a joist or a rafter,” consists of two adjoining illustrations: a plan‐type view on the left and a cross-section (section A–A) on the right. Together they show how two adjacent wood‐based sheathing panels are tied together where their edges do not lie over a supporting joist or rafter, using an intermediate batten and appropriately spaced mechanical fasteners.  

1. Left-hand view (plan/side elevation):  
  • At the very top is a horizontal rafter or joist, shown in cross-hatched fill. Below it lie two sheathing panels, each represented by a narrow rectangle abutting one another at their long edges.  
  • Along the span of the sheathing panels where they sit directly over the joist/rafter, evenly spaced through-nails (represented as black vertical lines) penetrate the panels into the joist. These illustrate the “elsewhere” spacing of 300 mm maximum for fasteners in areas supported by framing.  
  • At the central joint—where the panel edges meet but no underlying framing exists—a secondary vertical member (1) is fitted behind the butt joint. This is the batten, shown as a thicker vertical rectangle. Two short horizontal ticks on either side of the batten mark the positions of fasteners driven into it from each panel. These nails or screws must be of a type other than smooth nails, per EN 14592.  
  • A dimension arrow along the panel edges indicates a maximum fastener spacing of 150 mm along panel perimeters and joints.  

2. Right-hand view (section A–A):  
  • The topmost hatched strip again depicts the underside of the joist or rafter. Beneath it sits a continuous sheathing layer, cut away at the center to reveal the pair of panels (2) and (3) meeting at their ends.  
  • Label (1) denotes the batten fixed directly under the joint of panels 2 and 3. It is shown running horizontally in this section, sandwiched between the backs of both panels.  
  • Fastener group (2) represents nails or screws penetrating each panel into the hidden batten. These serve to clamp the two panel ends together, providing lateral load transfer in lieu of underlying framing.  
  • Fastener group (3), offset to the left, illustrates a conventional nail or screw driven through the panel into the primary joist/rafter above. It underscores the distinction between edge/joint fastener spacing (150 mm max.) and field fastener spacing (300 mm max.).  

Key points in context of EN 14592 and clause 9.2.3.2:  
  – Where sheathing panel edges do not overlie a structural member, panels must be joined by intermediate battens.  
  – Fasteners at these supported edges and joints must be ring-shank, thread-type or screws (i.e. non-smooth), spaced no more than 150 mm apart.  
  – In regions of continuous support (directly over joists or rafters), a reduced fastener density of up to 300 mm is permitted.  

Together, these two views illustrate proper detailing for ensuring diaphragm continuity and load distribution in timber‐framed assemblies when panel butt joints fall between main framing members.

(1) The simplified method of analysis given in 9.2.3.2 assumes that sheathing panels not supported by joists or rafters are connected to each other e.g. by means of battens as shown in Figure 10.1. Nails other than smooth nails, as defined in EN 14592, or screws should be used, with a maximum spacing along the edges of the sheathing panels of 150 mm. Elsewhere the maximum spacing should be 300 mm.

The image is an excerpt from a construction-standards manual, labelled “Figure 10.2 – Panel fixings.” It shows a pair of parallel vertical members (studs), with the space between them representing a panel face. Only the left stud is detailed with fixings; the right stud is shown as a simple vertical line. Both studs have “break” marks (jagged gaps) at their top and bottom, indicating that this is a partial view rather than a full-height elevation.

On the left stud face, two identical symbols denote fasteners (nails or screws). Each fastener is drawn as a simple filled circle. Between these two circles is a vertical, double-headed dimension arrow. The arrowlines terminate in small solid arrowheads that touch the center of each circle. Adjacent to that arrow is the annotation “(1),” which refers back to the accompanying text:
  • (1) corresponds to the maximum spacing of fixings along an internal stud, which should be no more than twice the edge spacing or 300 mm, whichever is lesser.
  
To the right of the studs is an area marked “(2).” Although the image cuts off much of its detail, the reference in the context text indicates that:
  • (2) refers to panel fixings along the panel edge, for which simplified methods prescribe a maximum fastener spacing of 150 mm for nails and 200 mm for screws.
  
Below the drawing, partly cropped, is additional text specifying:  
  – “nail spacing 300 mm to intermediate studs”  
  – “nail spacing 150 mm”  

Taken together with the nearby clauses (9.2.4.2, 9.2.4.3 and 10.9) the figure illustrates the two key spacing rules:  
  1. Along the panel edge (region (2)), fasteners must be no more than 150 mm apart if nails are used, or 200 mm apart if screws are used.  
  2. On intermediate or internal studs (region (1)), fastener spacing is limited to twice that edge spacing but must not exceed 300 mm under any circumstance.

Visually, the drawing is executed in clean black line work on a white background. The studs are rendered as narrow rectangles, the panel as a wider field, and the fixings as simple circles. The dimension arrow is centered between the circles, and each part reference number—(1) and (2)—is placed adjacent to the feature it annotates. Finally, the figure number and title “Figure 10.2 – Panel fixings” appear at the bottom center in bold type, signaling its role as a key illustration in the section on fastening requirements for timber-framed panels and trusses with punched metal plate connectors.

On internal studs the maximum spacing should be no more than twice the spacing along the edge or 300 mm, whichever is the lesser. See Figure 10.2.

The illustration is labeled “Figure A.1 – Example of block shear failure” and shows a steel-to-timber connection detail viewed in plan (looking into the end grain of the timber member). Two main elements are identified by reference numbers:  
 1. A steel connector plate (shown at the right by a simple solid-line outline and an arrow indicating the direction of the applied load parallel to the timber grain).  
 2. A rectangular timber block (shown to the left) into which multiple dowel-type fasteners (black filled circles) are driven.  

Fastener Layout and Numbering  
• Four fasteners form the top row, spaced horizontally from the timber’s left face toward the steel plate. Their center-to-center spacings are denoted ℓv,1, ℓv,2, ℓv,3 and ℓv,4, measured by arrowed double-headed lines above the top row.  
• Four fasteners form the bottom row, with horizontal spacings ℓv,5 through ℓv,8 marked below that row.  
• A middle row of two fasteners is located between the top and bottom rows; these anchor points lie centrally in the panel but are not dimensioned horizontally in this view.  

Block-shear Perimeter  
• A heavy dashed rectangle encloses the subset of fasteners closest to the steel plate, defining the hypothetical “block” of timber that might be torn out under combined tension and shear loading.  
• Along the deformed (tension) plane—which runs vertically from the bottom of the timber to the top—two vertical center-to-center spacings between rows are labeled ℓt,1 (between top and middle row) and ℓt,2 (between middle and bottom row), indicated by arrowed double-headed lines to the right of the fastener pattern.  

Dimensional Conventions  
• ℓv,i (i = 1 … 8) represent net widths in shear: the clear distances along the failure path parallel to the load direction, less fastener diameters.  
• ℓt,1 and ℓt,2 represent net lengths in tension: the clear distances along the path perpendicular to the load (i.e. along the timber grain), again net of fastener penetration.  

Connection Loading  
• A right-pointing arrow adjacent to the steel plate (element 1) shows the applied force component parallel to the timber grain, which tends to pull the enclosed block out of the timber.  
• Under such loading, block shear failure would involve:  
   – a tension failure along the vertical leg of the dashed perimeter (net tensile area Anet,t = ℓnet,t × t1), and  
   – a shear failure along the horizontal legs of the perimeter (net shear area Anet,v = ℓnet,v × t1),  

in accordance with the formulas given in Annex A of EN 1995-1-1. This figure thus visualizes the geometry used to calculate Fbs,Rk, the characteristic block shear capacity, combining both tensile and shear fracture areas around the fasteners.

The image presented is a two‐part line drawing illustrating a classic “plug shear” failure in a steel‐to‐timber dowel connection, as labeled “Figure A.2 – Example of plug shear failure.”  

Upper half (side‐elevation view):  
• A rigid horizontal plate (representing a steel connector) is shown in solid black atop a timber member.  
• A thick black arrow pointing to the left, drawn at the extreme left of the steel plate, indicates the direction of the applied load parallel to the timber grain.  
• Directly beneath the plate are a series of equally spaced dowel‐type fasteners (nails or bolts) represented by dark vertical rectangles penetrating the wood. Only the shanks are sketched – no heads or nuts are detailed.  
• Immediately to the right of the last illustrated fastener, a crack pattern is sketched in the timber, comprised of jagged, irregular lines that emanate from the dowel group and propagate downward and slightly to the right. This fracture outline defines the boundary of the “plug” of timber that is forced out under shear.  
• A double‐headed dimension arrow on the far right marks “tef” (effective penetration depth of the fastener or thickness of timber resisting shear), with one arrowhead at the underside of the steel connector and the other at the bottom of the timber section. A small label “tef” sits alongside this vertical dimension line.  

Lower half (three‐dimensional isometric view):  
• A rectangular prism of timber is shown in isometric projection, its top surface oriented toward the viewer.  
• In the center of its top face a U‐shaped recess has been cut out – the recess footprint matches the shape of the plug from the side view. Walls of the recess rise vertically from the bottom of the cavity to the original top surface.  
• The three‐sided cavity illustrates the actual piece of wood that has been “plugged” or sheared out under load, confirming the block‐shear geometry around the fasteners.  

Caption (centered beneath both views):  
Figure A.2 – Example of plug shear failure  

Overall, the drawing conveys how, under a load parallel to grain at the end of a timber member, a block of wood bounded by the fasteners and the free end can be sheared out as a unit (a “plug”). The side view ties back to EN 1995‐1‐1 plug‐shear failure formulas by showing the crack path and effective thickness tef, while the isometric block provides a clear visual of the volume of timber detached in that failure mode.

The illustration, labeled “Figure B.1,” presents three typical composite cross-section arrangements (stacked vertically) together with their corresponding bending‐stress profiles. All three sub-figures share the same general layout:

  • On the left: a schematic of the cross-section, showing individual parts (flanges, web or panels) identified by area Ai, moment of inertia Ii and elastic modulus Ei, together with key dimensional parameters bi (widths) and hi (depths) measured from the centroidal (neutral) axis. Two arrowed call-outs, marked (1) and (2), locate the rows of mechanical fasteners (e.g. nails, screws):  
    — (1) Fastener row at spacing s₁, slip-modulus K₁ under load F₁.  
    — (2) Fastener row at spacing s₃, slip-modulus K₃ under load F₃.  

  • On the right: the through-depth distribution of bending stresses (normal σ and shear τ). A linear variation of σ due to bending moment is superimposed on a parabolic shear‐stress diagram. Key notations:  
    – σ₁, σ₂, σ₃: extreme normal stresses at the top, middle, and bottom fiber respectively  
    – σₘ,1, σₘ,2, σₘ,3: mean normal stresses in each segment  
    – τₘₐₓ: maximum shear stress occurring at the neutral axis  

Subfigure 1 (top): Three-part section (e.g. box beam or built-up member)  
  – Parts A₁, A₂, A₃ stacked vertically.  
  – Widths b₁ (top flange), b₂ (web), b₃ (bottom flange).

     – Nailed:

       • η₂ = 3.0  
     – Bolted (a):

       • η₂ = 2.5

The input is “Table NA.2.2 — Recommended load-duration class assignment” from the National Annex to NS-EN 1995-1-1:2004+A2:2014 (Eurocode 5), and it establishes how different types of structural actions (loads) are grouped into duration classes for timber-structure design. In Eurocode 5 the design value of actions is modified by partial factors that depend, among other things, on how long a load persists. Table NA.2.2 therefore maps the “order of accumulated duration of characteristic load” to typical examples of actions, so that a designer can select the appropriate load-duration class and hence the correct modification factor γL.

1. Table structure  
   • Three columns:  
     1. “Load-duration class” (implicitly numbered 1 through 5 in order of descending duration)  
     2. “Order of accumulated duration of characteristic load” (time span over which the load is applied, summed over the life of the structure)  
     3. “Examples of loads” (common structural actions that fall into each duration bracket)  
   • Five rows corresponding to five duration classes. No numeric labels for class in the table excerpt, but in the Eurocode framework these correspond to Class 1 through Class 5.

2. Rows and their content  
   – Class 1 (very long duration)  
     • Accumulated duration: more than 10 years  
     • Examples: self-weight of structural members (dead loads, permanent actions)  
   – Class 2 (long duration)  
     • Accumulated duration: 6 months to 10 years  
     • Examples: storage loads (e.g. shelving, long-term occupancy)  
   – Class 3 (medium duration)  
     • Accumulated duration: 1 week to 6 months  
     • Examples: imposed floor loads, traffic loadsa (typical service loads in buildings and drive-on decks)  
   – Class 4 (short duration)  
     • Accumulated duration: less than 1 week  
     • Examples: snow loadsb (seasonal short-term loads) and traffic loads on bridges (concentrated, transient heavy vehicles)  
   – Class 5 (very short duration)  
     • Accumulated duration: less than 10 seconds  
     • Examples: wind loadsc (gusts), accidental loads (impact, shock)

   Footnotes in the original text explain that certain traffic loads may under special conditions be assigned to different classes, and that national choices (via the National Annex) may shift particular actions from one duration class to another.

3. Design context  
   • Clause NA 2.3.1.2(2)P of the National Annex directs users to assess Norwegian loads in accordance with this table.  
   • Load-duration class affects the partial factor for variable actions (γQ) and, in some cases, for permanent actions (γG), as specified elsewhere in the Annex.  
   • By assigning each load case to its correct duration class, the engineer ensures that the structural safety factors reflect both the magnitude and the temporal characteristics of the loads.  

4. Practical application  
   An engineer designing a glued-laminated timber beam carrying storage racks (accumulated occupancy ≥ 6 months) would categorize that imposed load in Class 2 and apply the corresponding γQ from Table NA 2.4.1. A snow load that typically persists only for days or weeks in winter falls into Class 4, yielding a smaller safety reduction (higher design effect) than a permanent dead load but a larger reduction than a very short-term wind gust.  

In summary, Table NA.2.2 codifies a simple but essential mapping: the longer a load acts on a timber structure over its service life, the more conservative the design factor. By grouping common structural loads into five duration classes, the table provides clear guidance for selecting partial factors in timber-structure calculations.

The excerpt presents Table NA.2.3 from the Norwegian National Annex to NS-EN 1995-1-1, which specifies the partial factors γM to be applied to material properties in ultimate limit‐state design. These factors adjust characteristic strengths to design values and vary by material or product type and by the combination of actions considered (ordinary vs. accidental). Below is a verbal “mapping” of the table’s structure and entries, together with notes on its intended use:

1. Table Title  
   “Table NA.2.3 — Partial factor for material property γM”

2. Column Headings  
   – Leftmost column: “Materialer og produkterᵃ” (Materials and products)  
   – Middle column: “γM — Ordinary ultimate limit state”  
   – Rightmost column: “γM — Ultimate limit state for accidental combinations”

3. Row Entries (material or product categories with corresponding γM values)

   a. Solid timber (all structural grades and strength classes)  
      • Ordinary ULS: γM = 1.25  
      • Accidental ULS: (not explicitly given in this row – see general note below)

   b. Glued laminated timber (GLT), parallel‐veneers and cross‐band veneers  
      • Ordinary ULS: γM = 1.15  
      • Accidental ULS: γM = 1.00

   c. Plywood (all types of wood‐based panels)  
      • Ordinary ULS: γM = 1.20  
      • Accidental ULS: 1.00

   d. Other wood‐based panels (e.g. particleboard, oriented strand board)  
      • Ordinary ULS: γM = 1.30  
      • Accidental ULS: 1.00

   e. Steel part of punched metal plate fasteners  
      • Ordinary ULS: γM = 1.30  
      • Accidental ULS: 1.00

   f. Fasteners (steel part, e.g. nails, screws, dowels)  
      • Ordinary ULS: γM = 1.10  
      • Accidental ULS: 1.00

4. Notes and Context  
   – Footnote ᵃ in the table points the reader to relevant product standards for detailed classification (e.g. EN 338 for timber, EN 1194 for GLT, EN 13986 for wood‐based panels).  
   – A general note below the table clarifies that for connections designed under Clause 8 (metal fasteners), this γM is to be used for the timber part; for other structural timber uses not covered by Clause 8, material partial factors are taken from the applicable product or structural standard.  
   – Cross‐laminated timber (CLT) is outside the primary scope but, if used, may typically adopt γM = 1.25 for ULS.  
   – The accidental combination factor (right column) is uniformly set to 1.00 unless a specific exception is noted.

5. Intended Application  
   – These γM values are multiplied into design formulae (e.g. stress checks, connection capacity calculations) to obtain design strengths.  
   – They reflect national calibration of material reliability and safety levels for Norway, in accordance with EN 1990 execution class requirements and NS 3516 guidance on execution of timber structures.

The table entitled “Table NA.7.2 — Examples of limiting values for deflections of beams” presents indicative span-to-deflection ratios for two kinds of structural elements (supports and beams) under three different deflection criteria. All deflection limits are given as ratios l/n, where l is the span or clear length of the member and n is the divisor defining the maximum permissible deflection.

1. General Layout  
   - The first (left-most) column identifies the element type.  
   - The next three columns give limiting deflection values for:  
     • winst — instantaneous deflection under imposed loads (short-term)  
     • wnet,fin — net final (long-term) deflection after creep and secondary effects  
     • wfin — total final deflection including immediate and long-term components  

2. Column Headings  
   • winst  
   • wnet,fin  
   • wfin  

3. Rows (Element Types)  
   A. Supports  
      • winst:   l/300 to l/500  
      • wnet,fin: l/250 to l/350  
      • wfin:    l/150 to l/300  
   B. Beams  
      • winst:   l/150 to l/250  
      • wnet,fin: l/125 to l/175  
      • wfin:    l/75  to l/150  

4. Interpretation of Ranges  
   - A lower ratio (for example l/150) permits larger deflection than a higher ratio (for example l/300).  
   - The two numbers in each cell define a recommended band: the first (smaller denominator) is the upper bound of permissible deflection, the second (larger denominator) is the lower bound, reflecting variability in use, stiffness, importance or aesthetic considerations.  
   - For “supports,” where deflections directly affect continuity and line of roof or floor, more stringent limits (higher denominators) are suggested.  
   - For “beams,” which may span larger distances between nodal supports, slightly looser limits are given.

5. How to Use in Design  
   - Identify span l of the support or beam under consideration.  
   - Decide which deflection limit applies:  
     • winst when checking immediate serviceability under live and dead loads;  
     • wnet,fin when accounting for creep and moisture-related long-term effects;  
     • wfin for the total combined deflection (often controlling for finishes or partitions).  
   - Select an appropriate ratio from the recommended range in the table. For instance, if you choose winst = l/200 for a beam of span 6 m, the maximum instantaneous deflection would be 6000 mm/200 = 30 mm.

6. Contextual Notes  
   - The National Annex indicates these values are “examples” and that the precise choice within each range may be set nationally or project-specifically.  
   - Where aesthetics or sensitive finishes are involved, use the more restrictive end of the range (e.g. l/150 for wfin on beams). For secondary spans or less visible areas, the looser end (e.g. l/300 for supports’ wfin) may be acceptable.  
   - These span-to-deflection limits form part of serviceability checks in EN 1995-1-1 (Eurocode 5) and its National Annex.

By laying out the table in this way, a designer or code-checking algorithm can rapidly map each structural member to its applicable serviceability limit, convert the span to an absolute deflection threshold, and verify compliance.

The image is a black-and-white schematic, drawn in plan (or elevation) view, illustrating the geometry of a block-shear failure path in a timber member loaded through a steel connector plate with multiple dowel-type fasteners. At the very bottom of the figure is the caption “Figure NA.A.1 — Example of block shear failure.”  

Overall layout  
• A large outer rectangle represents the cross-section outline of the timber member. Its longer dimension runs horizontally (left to right) and its shorter dimension runs vertically (top to bottom).  
• Concentric with the timber outline is a smaller, inset rectangle that represents the footprint of the steel connector plate (or packer) fixed to the timber. Two thin parallel lines at the right end of the inset rectangle further emphasize the plate thickness (t₁).  

Fastener arrangement  
• Within the bounds of the inset rectangle there are eight solid black circles arranged in two horizontal rows of four. These circles denote the locations of dowel-type fasteners (bolts, nails or screws) passing through the steel plate into the timber.  
• The top row of four dots lies adjacent to the upper edge of the plate; the bottom row of four dots lies adjacent to the lower edge of the plate. The two rows are separated by a clear vertical spacing.  

Fracture path  
• A continuous heavy line (“2” in the legend) marks the assumed block-shear fracture line. It starts at the outer top left corner of the inset plate, runs horizontally to the right past the last fastener in the top row, then turns downward at the plate’s outer right edge, and finally turns back to the left, passing beneath the bottom fastener row before closing at the lower left corner of the inset plate.  

Grain direction  
• An arrow marked “1” at the mid-height of the plate, on the left side, indicates the timber grain direction. The arrow points leftward, parallel to the top and bottom fracture segments, signifying that those segments lie parallel to grain (shear failure), while the vertical segment is transverse to grain (tension failure).  

Dimensional annotations  
• Along the top edge of the inset plate, immediately above the top fastener row, eight bidirectional horizontal dimension arrows label seven successive net shear lengths: ℓv,1 through ℓv,4 (between the left outer edge, individual fastener holes, and the right outer edge). These represent the net widths of shear planes parallel to the grain.  
• Along the bottom edge of the inset plate, directly beneath the bottom fastener row, a second set of eight bidirectional arrows label four more net shear lengths: ℓv,5 through ℓv,8. Together, ℓv,1 … ℓv,8 cover all shear lengths on both sides of the fracture path.  
• To the right of the inset plate, two vertical bidirectional arrows mark the two net tension lengths: ℓt,1 (between the top fracture segment and the plate’s midline) and ℓt,2 (between the midline and the bottom fracture segment). These correspond to the tensile ligament lengths perpendicular to the grain.  

Legend/key  
• In the lower-left corner of the drawing there is a simple key listing:  
 1 Grain direction  
 2 Fracture line  

Interpretation in context  
This diagram supports the block-shear capacity formula in Annex A of the Eurocode (NS-EN 1995-1-1), where the total shear area (sum of ℓv,i × t₁) and total tension area (sum of ℓt,i × t₁) are used to calculate characteristic block-shear resistance. The labeling of ℓv,1 … ℓv,8 and ℓt,1, ℓt,2 directly corresponds to the variables in equations A.3, A.6 and A.7, illustrating how to identify the net cross-sectional areas for both shear (parallel to grain) and tension (perpendicular to grain) fracture modes.

2. Lower schematic (isometric view of timber after plug shear):  
- A simple, three-dimensional rectangular block represents the timber member after failure has occurred. The block is drawn in perspective, with front, top, and right faces visible.  
- Within the top surface of that block is a U-shaped recess: two parallel vertical cuts from the top face taper into the body and meet a third cut at the back, forming a rectangular plug that appears to have been sheared out and removed. The sides of the recess are straight and the bottom of the cut is flat, leaving a “slot” whose geometry matches the locus of the bolt-row or fastener-row shear planes.  
- There are no fasteners shown in this lower view—only the void that represents the timber plug ejected by shear failure.  

Overall, this figure clarifies the plug-shear failure mode for a row of dowel-type fasteners loaded parallel to the wood grain near the end of a timber member. In Eurocode 5 terminology, the upper detail shows the stressed connection before and during shear, with effective embedment depth t_ef controlling the failure path. The lower is the post-failure timber block illustrating the characteristic “plug” that is forced out around the fastener group. This visual aids in understanding the geometry of the net shear area Anet,v and the failure mode referenced in Formula (NA.A.7), where the fastener’s penetration depth and timber thickness define the plug dimensions.
